Kubernetes is an open source container orchestration platform that automates many of the manual processes involved in deploying, managing, and scaling containerized applications.

Node Types: There are 2 types of nodes in the entire cluster: control plane (master) and compute plane (worker) nodes. Each node's components will be running only on their nodes, except kubelet, kube-proxy and CRI which runs as an agent/systemd service/daemonset in each and every node (both master & worker nodes). HA Setup: In HA (High availability environments) or multi-master setups for a large cluster, we deploy 3-5 control plane nodes and multiple worker nodes to run workloads for fault tolerance and reliability purposes.

In on-premise setups, we typically have 4 components in the control plane nodes, but in case of cloud-based setups, we will additionally have a cloud-controller manager (node, route, service controllers, etc.). 1. KUBE API SERVER:​ Role: Acts as the front-end component of the Kubernetes cluster and is the first point of contact for all client requests. Handles: Authentication (e.g., via username/password with LDAP, certificates, or tokens/IAM). Authorization (via RBAC, ABAC, Webhooks, or Node-based policies). Admission Control (Mutating & validating) and object schema Validation before persisting the workload object in the etcd. HA: In HA setups, the kube-API Server runs on multiple nodes with a load balancing mechanism. Communication: It communicates with all the other components (Kube Controller Manager, kube-scheduler, etcd) exclusively through authenticated requests. Execution & Port: By default, it runs as a static pod and listens on port 6443. (Request flow: API Request flow - API HTTP handler -> Auth/Authz -> Mutating Admission -> Object Schema Validation -> Validating Admission -> Persisted to etcd) 2. ETCD SERVICE​ etcd is a highly available, distributed, schemaless key-value store used to store all Kubernetes cluster data such as nodes, pods, config maps, secrets, service accounts, etc. It is used by components like Kubernetes, CoreDNS, Rook (Ceph), and more. etcd is written in Go and uses the RAFT consensus algorithm for high availability, fault tolerance, and consistency. Key Characteristics​ Key-Value Store: Stores data in simple key-value pairs (not documents or tables). Schema-less: Each key is independent. Updating one key doesn't affect others, unlike rigid schema designs in traditional SQL systems. Highly Available: In production, etcd is deployed on an odd number of nodes (e.g., 3 or 5) to ensure quorum-based leader election via RAFT. Cluster Communication: Client communication happens on port 2379. Peer (internal) communication between different etcd nodes happens on port 2380. Execution: Runs as a static pod on control plane nodes and is managed by kubelet (/etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml). Write Operations: Only the Kubernetes API Server performs write operations on etcd. Other components use the API Server to access the cluster state. etcd has its own command-line tool - etcdctl. Data Format: etcd stores all the Kubernetes cluster data in key/value format, for example: Key Value /registry/pods/default/nginx (Pod definition in JSON format) /registry/nodes/node1 (Node object data) /registry/configmaps/kube-system/coredns (CoreDNS ConfigMap) Commands:​ # To get etcdctl version ./etcdctl --version # To store a key-value pair (V2.0/V3.0) ./etcdctl set key1 value1 (V2.0) ./etcdctl put key1 value1 (v3.0) # To retrieve the stored data ./etcdctl get key1 # To list all keys ./etcdctl get "" --prefix --keys-only # To view more options ./etcdctl --help # Disaster Recovery: Regular etcd snapshots are essential. etcdctl snapshot save (Take a snapshot) etcdctl snapshot status (Check snapshot status) etcdctl snapshot restore (Restore a snapshot) 3. KUBE CONTROLLER MANAGER (KCM)​ Role: KCM will be having controllers/informers/watches, which ensures the desired state of the resource object stored in etcd matches the current state of the resource object in the cluster. It also informs the API Server if any discrepancies are found. Manages various controllers: Node Controller: Monitors the state of the node every 5s through API server. If it stops receiving heartbeats, the node is marked as unreachable but waits for 40 seconds before marking it unreachable. After a node is marked unreachable, it gives 5 minutes to come back up, and if it doesn't, it removes the pods associated with the nodes and provisions them to a healthy node. Replication Controller: Responsible for monitoring the status of replicasets, ensuring the desired number of pods are available anytime within the set. Job Controller ServiceAccount Controller Deployment Controller Execution & Port: Runs as a static pod and listens on port 10257. 4. CLOUD CONTROLLER MANAGER​ Role: Provides Kubernetes integration with cloud provider services (e.g., AWS, Azure). Handles: Node lifecycle management Route creation Load balancer and service management Functionality: Functions similarly to the Kube Controller Manager. Execution & Port: Runs as a static pod and also listens on port 10257. 5. KUBE SCHEDULER​ Role: Determines on which node a pod should be deployed based on: Available hardware resources Resource usage Affinity/anti-affinity rules Other node characteristics Note: It only decides/determines the node for the pods to be deployed on. The actual work is done by kubelet running on that node. If no suitable node is found or a node name mismatch happens, the pod status remains Pending. Process: It uses a four-step process: Pre-filter: Filter out all the nodes which are schedulable. Filtering nodes: Eliminate nodes that do not meet requirements. For example, eliminating the nodes that do not have sufficient CPU and memory requested by the POD. Scoring: Uses a priority function to assign a score (0-10) to eligible nodes to find the best fit. Reserve and bind: Reserve the workload object on the particular node and send a bind request to the Kube API Server, which then updates the pod spec with the node name. Execution & Port: Runs as a static pod and listens on port 10259.

1. KUBELET:​ Role: kubelet is the primary agent that runs on every node (both control and compute). Execution: It runs as a systemd service/daemonset (not a static pod) on each and every node in the cluster. Functionality: Once the kube-scheduler assigns a pod/workload to a node, kubelet pulls the necessary container images by communicating with the CR through CRI via gRPC v3 API and starts containers, thus creating the pods. It also sends regular pod status updates to kube-apiserver. Stores all Kubernetes configuration files under: /var/lib/kubelet Manages static pods (e.g., system-level/control plane node component pods like kube api server, etcd). Automatically restarts failed pods by recreating their containers inside that pod. Handles storage management for pod volumes. Port: By default, kubelet listens on port 10250. Note: Unlike other components, kubeadm does not deploy kubelet. The kubelet must be installed manually and running separately on each node before using kubeadm. 2. CRI (CONTAINER RUNTIME INTERFACE):​ Role: A plugin interface that allows kubelet (Kubernetes itself) to communicate with different container runtimes. Supported Runtimes: containerd (default runtime from Kubernetes v1.24+) Docker (deprecated from v1.24 onward) CRI-O Mirantis container runtime etc. OCI - Open Container Initiative​ imagespec (spec of how the image must be built) runtimespec (how any CR must be developed) crictl (ctr):​ Role: Tool maintained by the Kubernetes community to inspect and debug container runtimes. $ crictl $ crictl pull busybox $ crictl images $ crictl ps -a $ crictl exec -i -t 3e025dd50a72d956c4f14881fbb5b1080c9275674e95fb67f965f6478a957d60 ls $ crictl logs 3e025dd50a72d956c4f1 $ crictl pods containerd is now preferred over Docker due to lower latency and fewer abstraction layers (no need for dockershim). containerd is an official CNCF project. 3. KUBE PROXY​ Role: It is a process/systemd service/daemonset that runs on each node and looks for new services. Whenever a new service is created, it creates the appropriate rules on each node with the help of proxy modes to forward traffic/packets from those services to the backend pods. It acts like a traffic distributor. Functionality: Watches the control plane for updates on Services and EndpointSlices. Uses iptables or IPVS or userspace (depending on configuration) to route traffic to appropriate backend pods. Implements round-robin load balancing for service traffic. Ensures external and internal cluster traffic reaches the right pods based on the service definitions. Proxy Modes Supported: userspace (deprecated) iptables (Linux kernel-level packet filtering) IPVS (IP Virtual Server; more scalable and faster) Service Routing: When traffic is sent to a Service (via ClusterIP or DNS), kube-proxy routes the request to one of the backend pods using the defined proxy mode and load balancing strategy. (Diagram: Service Routing - Client Pod -> IP address for Service -> kube-proxy -> Backend Pod 1, 2, or 3)

Control plane​ Protocol Direction Port Range Purpose Used By TCP Inbound 6443 Kubernetes API server All TCP Inbound 2379-2380 etcd server client API kube-apiserver, etcd TCP Inbound 10250 Kubelet API Self, Control plane TCP Inbound 10259 kube-scheduler Self TCP Inbound 10257 kube-controller-manager Self Worker node(s)​ Protocol Direction Port Range Purpose Used By TCP Inbound 10250 Kubelet API Self, Control plane TCP Inbound 30000-32767 NodePort Services All
This detailed workflow describes the steps taken when a user submits a workload definition (e.g., a Deployment YAML) using kubectl.

Step 1: User Sends Request (kubectl → kube-apiserver)​ You run a command like: kubectl apply -f my-deploy.yaml kubectl sends an HTTPS request (e.g., a POST request for a new resource) to the kube-apiserver with the YAML payload (e.g., a Deployment resource). kube-apiserver performs: Validation of the schema. Authentication and Authorization. Serialization of the deployment object to JSON. Persistence of the object into etcd under a path like /registry/deployments/default/my-deploy. Method Purpose in REST kubectl equivalent Explanation GET Retrieve a resource kubectl get Reads info from the cluster (e.g., kubectl get pods) POST Create a new resource kubectl apply / kubectl create Sends a new object definition to the cluster PUT Replace an existing resource kubectl replace Completely overwrites an existing object PATCH Modify part of a resource kubectl patch Changes only specified fields of an object DELETE Remove a resource kubectl delete Deletes the object from etcd Step 2: kube-apiserver Writes to etcd​ kube-apiserver serializes the Deployment object to JSON and stores it in etcd using gRPC v3 API. etcd assigns a version and revision number, and sends an acknowledgment. kube-apiserver responds to kubectl with a 201 Created status. Step 3: Deployment Controller (in kube-controller-manager) Watches​ kube-controller-manager uses an informers or watches on Deployments via kube-apiserver. It sees the new Deployment object and creates the appropriate number of ReplicaSets with matching labels and desired replicas. It writes the ReplicaSet object back to the API server, which stores it in etcd. Step 4: ReplicaSet Controller Reacts​ The kube-controller-manager also runs the ReplicaSet Controller. It watches ReplicaSets, sees the new ReplicaSet, and creates the required number of Pod objects. It sends the Pod objects to the API server, where they are stored in etcd. At this point, the Pod objects exist in etcd but are in a Pending state and not assigned to a node. Step 5: kube-scheduler Watches for Unscheduled Pods​ kube-scheduler watches the API server for Pods without .spec.nodeName (i.e., unscheduled Pods). It sees the unscheduled Pod and uses the 4-step scheduling process: Filters eligible nodes: (Based on taints, resources, affinity). Scores and ranks nodes: Assigns a score (0-10) to eligible nodes. Selects the best node: The highest scoring node. Sends a Bind request to API server: A POST /bind request with the Pod name and the selected node. Step 6: kube-apiserver Updates .spec.nodeName​ The API server updates the Pod object with the chosen .spec.nodeName = node-X. This update triggers an etcd write and an event for all watchers (including the kubelet on node-X). Step 7: kubelet on node-X Watches Pods​ The kubelet on node-X runs a watch on the API server for Pods assigned to its node. It sees the new Pod with nodeName = node-X. Step 8: kubelet Pulls Image & Prepares Environment​ kubelet: Verifies the Pod specification and creates sandboxes (namespaces, cgroups) for the Pod. It calls the Container Runtime (containerd or another CRI) via gRPC to: Pull the container image. Start the container. It uses a CNI plugin (e.g., Calico, Flannel) to assign an IP and set up networking for the Pod. Step 9: kubelet Sends Pod Status Updates​ kubelet continuously monitors the Pod/container. It sends regular POST /status calls to the API server with the status update (e.g., Pending → Running → Terminated), IP addresses, and Probe results. Step 10: kubelet Runs Health Checks​ kubelet performs continuous health checks on the running container: Liveness Probes: If failing, it restarts the container. Readiness Probes: If failing, it removes the Pod from the service load balancer (via the Endpoint Controller). Step 11: Endpoint Controller Updates Services​ If the Pod becomes Ready, the Endpoints Controller (from kube-controller-manager) updates the associated Endpoints or EndpointSlices. It also removes unhealthy pods from the endpoints. This update is crucial for enabling load balancing via the kube-proxy or Ingress controller. Step 12: kube-proxy Updates IPTables/IPVS​ On each node, kube-proxy watches for updates to Services and Endpoints. Whenever a Service is created or updated, it programs IPTables or IPVS rules to forward traffic from the Service's ClusterIP to the Pod's IP addresses. Step 13: Final Running State​ At this stage: The container is running. The Service is routing traffic to the container. kubelet ensures continuous health checks. Metrics, logs, and events related to the Pod are available to the user.
Before diving into Kubernetes security (RBAC, Secrets, TLS), it’s essential to understand encryption—the backbone of all secure communication.
documents.s: Authentication: Encryption, TLS, and Secure Key Exchange

documents.t: Encryption converts readable data (plaintext) into unreadable (ciphertext) to ensure only authorized access.

Confidentiality: Protect sensitive data in transit (network) and at rest (storage). Integrity: Prevent tampering during transmission. Authenticity: Verify the identity of the sender and receiver. Non-repudiation: Prevent a party from denying they sent a message.

Definition: Uses one secret key for both encryption and decryption. Characteristics: Fast and efficient — ideal for bulk data. Tooling: AES (Industry standard), ChaCha20. Risk: "Key Exchange Problem"—if the key is intercepted while being shared, all data is exposed. K8s Use Case: Disk & database encryption (AES-256), Kubernetes Secrets at rest.

Definition: Uses a key pair: a Public key (shared with everyone) and a Private key (kept secret). Logic: Data encrypted with the Public key can only be decrypted by the corresponding Private key. Tooling: RSA, Ed25519, ECC. Primary Tools: ssh-keygen: Specifically for SSH authentication. openssl: The standard toolkit for TLS certificate management and identity validation. Use Case: Authentication, digital signatures, and secure key exchange.

Feature Symmetric Asymmetric Keys Used One shared key Public + Private key pair Speed Very Fast Slower (Mathematical overhead) Security Key sharing is risky Secure exchange (Private key never moves) Primary Use Bulk data encryption Authentication, exchanging session keys Examples AES, ChaCha20 RSA, SSH, TLS, Certificates

Protects data while moving (client $\leftrightarrow$ server, pod $\leftrightarrow$ pod). Mechanism: Uses TLS (Transport Layer Security) or mTLS. K8s Examples: HTTPS traffic, kubectl $\leftrightarrow$ API server, Istio service mesh.
Protects stored data (volumes, databases, backups). Mechanism: Uses AES / KMS (Key Management Service). K8s Examples: EBS volume encryption, etcd Secrets encryption.

To manage security, you must identify the Client and the Server: Client: The entity that initiates a request (e.g., a Developer running kubectl, or a Pod fetching data). Server: The entity that responds to the request (e.g., the kube-apiserver, or a database like etcd).
SSH uses asymmetric encryption to prove identity without sending a password over the network.

When you connect for the first time (ssh user@ip), the server sends its Host Public Key. TOFU (Trust on First Use): You accept the fingerprint, and it is stored in ~/.ssh/known_hosts. If the server is reinstalled or spoofed later, the fingerprint won't match, triggering a security warning.

Generate Keys: Use ssh-keygen -t ed25519. This creates a private key (id_ed25519) and a public key (id_ed25519.pub). Copy Public Key: You place your public key on the server in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys. The Challenge: The server sends a random string encrypted with your public key. Only your Private Key (which never leaves your local machine) can decrypt it. Once decrypted, you are authenticated.
HTTPS uses a Hybrid approach: Asymmetric to securely exchange a key, then Symmetric for fast data transfer.
documents.s: 6. Deep Dive: How TLS/HTTPS Works (The Hybrid Approach)

documents.t: Request: Browser/Client requests a secure connection. Presentation: Server sends its TLS Certificate (contains the Server's Public Key + CA Signature). Verification: Browser verifies the certificate via a Trusted Certificate Authority (CA). Key Exchange: Browser generates a random Symmetric Session Key. It encrypts this key with the Server’s Public Key and sends it. Decryption: The Server uses its Private Key to decrypt the session key. Secure Tunnel: Now, both sides have the same Symmetric key and use it for fast, encrypted data transfer.

In standard TLS, only the server proves its identity. In mTLS, the client also presents a certificate to the server. This is used extensively in Kubernetes for internal communication (e.g., kubelet $\leftrightarrow$ api-server).

HSMs: Use Hardware Security Modules for physical key protection. Cloud KMS: Use AWS KMS or Azure Key Vault for centralized, encrypted storage. Air-Gapped Systems: Keep root CA keys offline. Rotation: Regularly rotate certificates and private keys.

Extension Description .pub SSH Public Key (Safe to share). .key / .pem Private Key (Must be kept secret). .crt / .cer Signed TLS Certificate. .csr Certificate Signing Request (Sent to a CA to get a cert).

Certificate Type Use Case Trust Level Typical Use Public CA Internet-facing websites. Trusted by all browsers. Production web apps. Private CA Internal corporate services. Trusted only within the org. Microservices, K8s internal auth. Self-Signed Local development. Not trusted by browsers. Testing, local environment.

Symmetric = Speed: Use for bulk data. Asymmetric = Identity: Use for the handshake and authentication. TLS = Hybrid: Uses both to be both secure and fast. mTLS: Standard for Kubernetes internal security (both sides verify each other). Encryption: At-Rest and In-Transit must both be enabled for a hardened system.
This guide outlines the process of granting a new user (Seema) access to a Kubernetes cluster using Certificate Signing Requests (CSR) and X.509 client certificates.

1. Seema Generates a Private Key​ openssl genrsa -out seema.key 2048 Description: Creates a 2048-bit RSA private key. This file must remain confidential as it proves the user's identity. 2. Seema Generates a CSR​ openssl req -new -key seema.key -out seema.csr -subj "/CN=seema" Description: Generates a Certificate Signing Request. The Common Name (CN) is set to seema, which Kubernetes will interpret as the username. 3. Seema Sends CSR to Admin (Base64 Encoded)​ cat seema.csr | base64 | tr -d "\n" Description: Encodes the CSR into a single-line Base64 string so the Administrator can paste it into a Kubernetes YAML manifest.

4. Admin Creates the CSR Object in Kubernetes​ The Admin creates a CertificateSigningRequest manifest: apiVersion: certificates.k8s.io/v1 kind: CertificateSigningRequest metadata: name: seema spec: request: <BASE64_ENCODED_CSR> signerName: kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-client expirationSeconds: 7776000 usages: - client auth request: The Base64 string generated in Step 3. signerName: Instructs Kubernetes to treat this as a client authentication request. usages: Defines the cert for client authentication. expirationSeconds: Sets validity to 90 days (7,776,000 seconds). 5. Admin Approves CSR​ kubectl certificate approve seema Description: Kubernetes signs the request using the cluster's CA and issues the certificate. 6. Admin Retrieves the Signed Certificate​ kubectl get csr seema -o jsonpath='{.status.certificate}' | base64 -d > seema.crt Description: Extracts the signed certificate from the CSR object, decodes it, and saves it as seema.crt. This file is then sent back to Seema.
documents.s: Phase 2: Administrator Approves and Issues Certificate

documents.t: 7. Seema Configures kubeconfig​ Add credentials: kubectl config set-credentials seema \ --client-certificate=seema.crt \ --client-key=seema.key \ --certificate-authority=ca.crt \ --embed-certs=true Add cluster info: kubectl config set-cluster kind-my-second-cluster \ --server=https://127.0.0.1:59599 \ --certificate-authority=ca.crt \ --embed-certs=true \ --kubeconfig=~/.kube/config Create context: kubectl config set-context seema@kind-my-second-cluster-context \ --cluster=kind-my-second-cluster \ --user=seema \ --namespace=default

8. Admin Creates Role and RoleBinding​ Even with a certificate, the user has no permissions by default. The Admin must apply RBAC: kind: Role apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 metadata: namespace: default name: seema-role rules: - apiGroups: [""] resources: ["pods"] verbs: ["get", "list", "delete"] kubectl create rolebinding seema-binding \ --role=seema-role \ --user=seema \ --namespace=default Description: This allows Seema to get, list, and delete pods in the default namespace. 9. Admin Validates Access​ kubectl auth can-i delete pods --namespace=default --as=seema Description: Simulates Seema's permissions to verify the RBAC configuration before she starts using the cluster. 10. Seema Activates Her Context​ kubectl config use-context seema@kind-my-second-cluster-context Description: Switches kubectl to use her new credentials and context.

Access via REST API: curl https://<API-SERVER-IP>:<PORT>/api/v1/namespaces/default/pods \ --cacert ca.crt --cert seema.crt --key seema.key Using an alternate kubeconfig file: kubectl get pods --kubeconfig=myconfig.yaml 11. Check Certificate Expiration​ openssl x509 -noout -dates -in seema.crt Description: Displays the validity period (NotBefore and NotAfter) of the issued certificate.

The kubeconfig file is a configuration file used to configure access to Kubernetes clusters. It stores: Cluster details: API server URL, Certificate Authority (CA) certificates. User credentials: Authentication tokens, client certificates, and private keys. Contexts: Specific combinations of a cluster, a user, and (optionally) a namespace. Why is it used? It enables kubectl to securely access clusters without requiring manual input (like server URLs or credentials) for every command. Without it, the process of communicating with the API server would be lengthy, manual, and error-prone.

A context in kubeconfig links a cluster, a user, and a namespace. It allows for quick switching between different environments. Example: A user named Seema can define three contexts to manage different environments: seema@dev-cluster-context seema@staging-cluster-context seema@prod-cluster-context Each context simplifies management by specifying which cluster to talk to, which user credentials to use, and which namespace to target (e.g., app1-dev-ns, app1-staging-ns, app1-prod-ns).

Typically stored at ~/.kube/config, the file includes: Clusters: Defines the API server endpoint and the CA certificate used to verify the server. Users: Includes client certificates and private keys used to authenticate the user to the cluster. Contexts: The mapping that combines cluster and user settings. Current-context: Indicates which context is currently active for kubectl commands. Key Certificate Data Fields: certificate-authority-data: Verifies the API server’s identity to the client. client-certificate-data: Authenticates the user to the API server. client-key-data: Proves the user’s identity securely. (Note: These fields contain Base64-encoded data).

apiVersion: v1 kind: Config # Define the clusters clusters: - name: dev-cluster # Logical name for the development cluster cluster: server: https://dev-cluster-api-server:6443 # API server endpoint certificate-authority-data: <certificate-data> # Base64-encoded CA certificate - name: staging-cluster cluster: server: https://staging-cluster-api-server:6443 certificate-authority-data: <certificate-data> - name: prod-cluster cluster: server: https://prod-cluster-api-server:6443 certificate-authority-data: <certificate-data> # Define users (credentials for authentication) users: - name: seema # Logical user name user: client-certificate-data: <client-cert-data> # Base64-encoded client certificate client-key-data: <client-key-data> # Base64-encoded private key # Define contexts (combination of cluster + user + optional namespace) contexts: - name: seema@dev-cluster-context context: cluster: dev-cluster user: seema namespace: app1-dev-ns # Default namespace for this context - name: seema@staging-cluster-context context: cluster: staging-cluster user: seema namespace: app1-staging-ns - name: seema@prod-cluster-context context: cluster: prod-cluster user: seema namespace: app1-prod-ns # Set the default context to use current-context: seema@dev-cluster-context

Task Command View current context kubectl config current-context List all contexts kubectl config get-contexts Switch context kubectl config use-context <context-name> View config kubectl config view Set default namespace kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=<ns> Add new user kubectl config set-credentials <user> --client-certificate=<cert> --client-key=<key> Add new cluster kubectl config set-cluster <cluster> --server=<url> --certificate-authority=<ca> Add new context kubectl config set-context <context> --cluster=<cluster> --user=<user> --namespace=<ns> Delete context kubectl config delete-context <context> Rename context kubectl config rename-context <old> <new>

You can manage multiple configuration files without merging them into one: Using the flag: kubectl get pods --kubeconfig=~/.kube/dev-kubeconfig Using the environment variable: export KUBECONFIG=$HOME/.kube/config:$HOME/.kube/custom-kubeconfig This ensures kubectl automatically uses and merges the specified configuration files. Adding Entries Safely: Always use kubectl config commands to add clusters, users, or contexts instead of editing the file manually. This ensures data integrity and proper certificate embedding. Example sequence: Add a user Add a cluster Add a context Switch to the context Verify configuration using kubectl config view --minify

mTLS enhances standard TLS by requiring both the client and the server to authenticate each other using certificates. This ensures mutual trust and secure communication between machines and services. Standard TLS (1-Way): Only the server presents a certificate (typical for public websites). mTLS (2-Way): Both sides present and verify certificates. This is ideal for Kubernetes internal service-to-service communication. Managed Kubernetes services (EKS, GKE, AKS) use mTLS by default for internal communication between components like the kube-apiserver, kubelet, and etcd. TLS (1-Way) vs. mTLS (2-Way)​ Feature TLS (1-Way) mTLS (2-Way) Authentication Server only Both client and server Use Case Public websites, APIs Microservices, Kubernetes, APIs w/ clients Identity Verification Server proves identity Mutual identity verification Certificate Required Only server certificate Both server and client certificates
Clusters secure communication between components using TLS certificates—and these are typically signed by an internal private Certificate Authority (CA).

Internal Trust: Internal components don’t need public browser trust. Efficiency: Faster issuance and rotation of certificates. Automation: Certificates are often short-lived and auto-generated by the cluster during initialization.

Strategy Advantages Used For Single private CA Simple management Most standard clusters Multiple CAs Isolates trust, reduces blast radius Large-scale or high-security clusters (Often etcd has a separate CA) Why separate etcd CA? etcd stores the full cluster state. Isolating its CA limits the impact if the main Kubernetes CA is compromised.

kubeadm, k3s, GKE, EKS, AKS: Private CAs are automatically generated. Kubernetes-the-Hard-Way: The administrator manually creates the root CA and signs all certificates. Do Enterprises Use Public CAs Internally? No. Public CAs are only used for public-facing services (Ingress, Load Balancers, Gateway API). All Kubernetes internal component communication relies on private CAs.

Key idea: The role (Client vs. Server) depends on who initiates the connection. Component Acts As Communicates With kubectl Client API Server Scheduler Client API Server Controller-manager Client API Server Kube-proxy Client API Server Kubelet Client or Server Client when reporting to API server; Server when API server fetches logs/exec. API Server Server or Client Server for all clients; Client when calling etcd or kubelets. etcd Always Server API server only Examples: Kubelet reporting node status: Kubelet is the client, API server is the server. kubectl logs: API server connects to the kubelet; API server is the client, Kubelet is the server.

documents.t: To understand the TLS flow, everything required is stored in three main locations: Static pod manifests: /etc/kubernetes/manifests Kubeconfig files: /etc/kubernetes/*.conf (or inside pods) Kubelet directories: /var/lib/kubelet/

Purpose Path API server / scheduler / controller configs /etc/kubernetes/*.conf Static pod manifests /etc/kubernetes/manifests CA & certs for control plane /etc/kubernetes/pki etcd certs /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd Kubelet certs /var/lib/kubelet/pki Kube-proxy kubeconfig (in pod) /var/lib/kube-proxy

1. Server-Side (API Server) Inspect the static pod manifest: cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml Flag: --tls-cert-file=/etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.crt Check the certificate: openssl x509 -in /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.crt -text -noout Subject: CN=kube-apiserver Issuer: CN=kubernetes 2. How Scheduler Trusts API Server The scheduler uses a kubeconfig file: cat /etc/kubernetes/scheduler.conf Field: certificate-authority-data: <base64> Decoding this shows the cluster root CA. The scheduler uses it to validate the API server’s certificate. 3. Client-Side (Scheduler Auth to API Server) The same scheduler.conf contains: client-certificate-data client-key-data Decoded certificate: Subject: CN=system:kube-scheduler Issuer: CN=kubernetes 4. How API Server Verifies Scheduler In kube-apiserver.yaml: Flag: --client-ca-file=/etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt Any client certificate signed by ca.crt is trusted.

1. etcd Server Certificate cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml Flags: --cert-file=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt --key-file=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key --client-cert-auth=true --trusted-ca-file=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt Inspect: openssl x509 -in /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt -text -noout Subject: CN= Issuer: CN=etcd-ca 2. How API Server Verifies etcd In kube-apiserver.yaml: Flag: --etcd-cafile=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt 3. API Server Client Certificate to etcd In kube-apiserver.yaml: --etcd-certfile=/etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver-etcd-client.crt --etcd-keyfile=/etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver-etcd-client.key Certificate: Subject: CN=kube-apiserver-etcd-client Issuer: CN=etcd-ca

Kubelet is NOT a Pod; it is a systemd process. Find Config: ps -ef | grep kubelet Flag: --config=/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml Kubelet Certificates: /var/lib/kubelet/pki/kubelet.crt /var/lib/kubelet/pki/kubelet.key Inspect: openssl x509 -in /var/lib/kubelet/pki/kubelet.crt -text -noout Subject: CN=system:node:, O=system:nodes Issuer: CN= How Kubelet Got This Cert: Initially authenticates via bootstrap token. Submits a CSR (Certificate Signing Request). API server approves and signs. Kubelet obtains its long-term certificate. Does API Server validate Kubelet server certificate? Not strictly. The API server already authenticated the node during bootstrap and issued its cert. Authorization protections (RBAC, Node authorizer, NodeRestriction) restrict behavior. API Server’s Client Certificate to Kubelet: Flags in kube-apiserver.yaml: --kubelet-client-certificate=/etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver-kubelet-client.crt --kubelet-client-key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver-kubelet-client.key Subject: CN=kube-apiserver-kubelet-client

Admission Controllers act as gatekeepers that intercept requests to the Kubernetes API server after the request is authenticated and authorized, but before the object is persisted to etcd. They are critical for enforcing security, governance, and operational standards. Admission controllers can modify, validate, or reject requests based on custom logic or cluster policies. They apply only to write operations (CREATE, UPDATE, DELETE) and have no effect on read operations (GET, LIST, WATCH).

Authentication (AuthN): Verifies the identity of the requester (User/ServiceAccount). Authorization (AuthZ): Verifies if the identity has permission to perform the action (e.g., RBAC). Admission Control: Intercepts the request to validate or modify the object content. Persistence: If all checks pass, the object is written to etcd. Key Concept: Admission controllers act as gatekeepers for object persistence. Even if a user has RBAC permissions to create a Pod, an admission controller can reject the request if the Pod configuration violates cluster policy (e.g., trying to run as root).
documents.s: A typical API request travels through the following phases:

documents.t: Action: Modify incoming requests before they are stored. Purpose: Set default values, inject sidecar containers, or alter configuration to meet standards. Order: Executed before validating controllers. Plugin Description Enabled by Default MutatingAdmissionWebhook Sends incoming objects to an external webhook before persistence. Used for tasks like auto-injecting sidecars (e.g., Istio proxies). Commonly applies default labels, runtime constraints, and security settings. Yes DefaultStorageClass Assigns a default StorageClass to PersistentVolumeClaims lacking one, ensuring PVCs use appropriate backends like EBS, GCP PD, or Azure Disk. Yes DefaultTolerationSeconds Sets default tolerations for Pods exposed to NoExecute taints, preventing unwanted evictions when tolerations are missing. Yes DefaultIngressClass Assigns a default IngressClass when none is specified to avoid confusion in multi-ingress setups. Yes

Action: Inspect requests and accept or reject them. They do not modify the object. Purpose: Enforce compliance, security policies, and quotas. Order: Executed after mutating controllers. Plugin Description Enabled by Default NodeRestriction Prevents kubelets from modifying resources outside their own node, strengthening node-level security boundaries. Yes ValidatingAdmissionWebhook Sends API objects to external validation webhooks, often used for compliance checks, such as disallowing privileged containers. Yes PodSecurity Enforces Pod Security Standards (Privileged, Baseline, Restricted), blocking Pods violating rules like running as root. This replaces deprecated PodSecurityPolicies (PSPs). No (opt-in) ResourceQuota Enforces namespace-level quotas for CPU, memory, and storage, preventing resource overconsumption in multi-tenant clusters. Yes NamespaceLifecycle Disallows operations in nonexistent or terminating namespaces, preventing object creation during namespace teardown. Yes

Action: Perform both mutation and validation. Example: LimitRanger applies default resource limits (mutation) and checks if limits are within allowed ranges (validation). Plugin Mutating Validating Description Enabled by Default LimitRanger Yes Yes Sets default CPU/memory requests and limits and validates they fall within allowed ranges for fair scheduling. Yes AlwaysPullImages Yes Yes Forces Pods to always pull images from the registry, preventing the use of potentially tampered local images. No ServiceAccount Yes Yes Assigns default ServiceAccounts and validates Pods use authorized ones, ensuring proper identity and access control. Yes
When built-in logic is insufficient, Kubernetes allows the use of Admission Webhooks. These are HTTP callbacks that receive admission requests and return a decision.

Webhook Server: A service (usually running in-cluster) that contains the custom logic. Configuration: MutatingWebhookConfiguration or ValidatingWebhookConfiguration resources tell the API server where to send requests. Process: API Server sends the JSON object to the Webhook Server. Webhook Server reviews the object. Webhook Server returns a response: allowed: true/false (for validation) or a JSON Patch (for mutation).
OPA Gatekeeper: Uses Rego language for policy enforcement. Kyverno: Kubernetes-native policy engine (uses YAML).

Admission plugins are configured in the kube-apiserver manifest: (/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml). --enable-admission-plugins: Adds plugins to the default list. --disable-admission-plugins: Removes plugins from the default list. Example: --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction,MutatingAdmissionWebhook,ValidatingAdmissionWebhook Note on Kubeadm/KIND Defaults: In clusters bootstrapped with kubeadm (including KIND), many admission controllers (like LimitRanger, DefaultStorageClass, ResourceQuota) are enabled by default even if not explicitly listed. You must use --disable-admission-plugins to turn them off.

The API server executes admission controllers in a strict order: Mutating Phase: All enabled Mutating controllers run first (serial execution). The object is modified in memory. If a Mutating controller rejects a request, the process stops, and the request fails. Validating Phase: All enabled Validating controllers run next (serial execution). These controllers check the final state of the object (after all mutations). If any Validating controller rejects the request, the entire request is denied, and nothing is written to etcd. Persistence: If all controllers pass, the object is persisted to etcd.

Stage: Authorization (before Admission). Input Data: Only receives request attributes (User, Group, Namespace, Verb, Resource Type). Blind Spot: It cannot see the content of the object (e.g., Pod image, labels, container specs). Use Case: Context-aware access control (e.g., "Allow access only from corporate VPN IP," "Deny deletions outside business hours"). Prevalence: Rare in standard deployments; standard RBAC is usually sufficient.

Stage: Admission Control (after AuthZ). Input Data: Receives the full Kubernetes object (Pod specs, Ingress configurations, etc.). Capabilities: Can Validate (Accept/Reject) and Mutate (Modify). Use Case: Governance and Security (e.g., "Reject Pods using images from public registries," "Enforce 'Team' label on all Deployments"). Prevalence: Standard for enterprise policy enforcement.

The Kubernetes API is the primary interface for all cluster operations, enabling interaction with resources like Pods, Services, and Deployments. The API server acts as the central gatekeeper, managing Authentication (AuthN), Authorization (AuthZ), and Admission Control. Kubernetes API: The logical interface (RESTful endpoints) exposing cluster resources. API Server: The physical component (pod/process) that hosts the API. It handles authentication, authorization, schema validation, and admission control before persisting data to etcd.
The API is a RESTful, resource-based interface utilizing standard HTTP verbs (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH).

The API server exposes various paths for different functionalities: Endpoint Description Access Type /version Returns API server version. Unauthenticated /healthz, /livez, /readyz Health checks for the API server. Unauthenticated /api Root path for the Core Group (legacy resources). Authenticated /apis Root path for Named Groups (modern/modular resources). Authenticated /metrics Exposes Prometheus-format metrics. Authenticated /logs Not a standalone endpoint. kubectl logs interacts with the Kubelet's /containerLogs/ endpoint. N/A

Kubernetes splits resources into groups for modularity and versioning. 1. Core Group​ Path: /api/v1 YAML Representation: apiVersion: v1 Resources: Pods, Services, ConfigMaps, Secrets, Namespaces, PVs, PVCs. Note: The group name is an empty string (""), which is why it does not appear in the YAML apiVersion. 2. Named Groups​ Path: /apis/<GROUP>/<VERSION> YAML Representation: apiVersion: <GROUP>/<VERSION> Resources: apps/v1: Deployments, StatefulSets, DaemonSets. rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1: Roles, RoleBindings. networking.k8s.io/v1: Ingress, NetworkPolicies. Note: API path format: /<root>/<group>/<version>/namespaces/<namespace>/<resourceType>/<name>

Direct Access (curl): Requires manual certificate management. Example: curl https://<IP>:6443/api --cert client.crt --key client.key --cacert ca.crt Unauthenticated Access: Useful for health checks. Example: curl -k https://<IP>:6443/healthz Kubectl Proxy: Creates a local HTTP server that handles authentication and forwards requests to the API server over HTTPS. Command: kubectl proxy -> Access via http://127.0.0.1:8001
After Authentication verifies identity, Authorization determines if the identity has permission to perform the requested action.
User/Group: Who is making the request. Verb: Action (get, list, create, delete). Resource: Object type (pods, secrets). Namespace: Scope of the resource. API Group: The group the resource belongs to.

Kubernetes supports pluggable authorization modules. The API server evaluates these modes in the order specified by the --authorization-mode flag. 1. RBAC (Role-Based Access Control)​ The standard for production environments. It grants permissions based on roles assigned to users/groups. Role: Defines permissions within a specific namespace. RoleBinding: Assigns a Role to a user/group/SA within a namespace. ClusterRole: Defines permissions cluster-wide (or for non-namespaced resources). ClusterRoleBinding: Assigns a ClusterRole to a user/group/SA cluster-wide. 2. ABAC (Attribute-Based Access Control)​ Mechanism: Uses a static JSON policy file defined at API server startup. Drawback: Any policy change requires restarting the API server. Status: Deprecated; not recommended for production. 3. Webhook Authorization​ Outsources the authorization decision to an external service (e.g., OPA, Gatekeeper). Process: API server sends a JSON payload of the request to a remote endpoint. The endpoint returns Allow or Deny. Use Case: Complex business logic, dynamic rules, or centralized policy management. 4. Node Authorization​ A specialized mode that restricts kubelet permissions. Function: Ensures a kubelet on a specific node can only read/modify resources (Pods, Secrets, ConfigMaps) scheduled on that specific node. Mechanism: Activated automatically; relies on the kubelet's identity. 5. AlwaysAllow / AlwaysDeny​ AlwaysAllow: Permits every request. No security. AlwaysDeny: Rejects every request. Use Case: Strictly for testing or debugging; never for production.
Authorization modes are configured in the API server manifest: /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml. Example Configuration: --authorization-mode=Node,Webhook,RBAC

Modes are checked sequentially. The first module to give a definitive decision halts the chain. Decision Consequence Allow Request is authorized; process stops. Deny Request is rejected; process stops. No Opinion Evaluation proceeds to the next configured mode.

Configuration: Node, Webhook, RBAC Node Authorizer: Checks request. Since Seema is not a Kubelet, it returns No Opinion. Webhook Authorizer: External service checks metadata (time of day, user group, source IP). If policy violated: Returns Deny. If policy valid: Returns No Opinion (or Allow). RBAC Authorizer: Checks RoleBindings. If Seema has a Role permitting create pods: Returns Allow. If no Role found: Returns Deny.

RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) regulates access to Kubernetes resources by defining who can perform what actions on which resources and where (namespace or cluster). RBAC consists of four objects: RBAC Object Scope Purpose Role Namespace Define permissions within a namespace RoleBinding Namespace Assign Role/ClusterRole to subjects within a namespace ClusterRole Cluster Define cluster-wide or reusable permissions ClusterRoleBinding Cluster Bind ClusterRole to subjects cluster-wide Subjects: Users, Groups, ServiceAccounts.

Resource Type Examples Notes Namespaced pods, deployments, configmaps, secrets Access controlled by Role + RoleBinding Cluster-scoped nodes, PVs, namespaces Require ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding Check resources: kubectl api-resources kubectl api-resources -o wide

Kubernetes has no built-in user database. Human users authenticate via: TLS certificates External identity providers (OIDC, LDAP/Kerberos via proxies/webhooks) Static password or token files (legacy/unsupported for production) Kubernetes does manage ServiceAccounts, which are the primary identities for non-human clients (pods, automation tools, controllers). Authentication is always performed by the API server, regardless of the mechanism used.
CSV format: password,username,uid,"groups" Enabled via: --basic-auth-file=<path> Requires: API server restart. Security: Not secure (plaintext, no rotation). Not recommended for production.
CSV format: token,username,uid,"groups" Enabled via: --token-auth-file=<path> Security: No rotation, insecure.

Used by pods and external automation. Represented as bearer tokens in requests. Stored in pods at: /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token JWT signed by API server private key. Token types: Projected tokens (short-lived, auto-rotated) Manually requested short-lived tokens Legacy secret-based long-lived tokens (deprecated)
Strong, recommended for human users and system components. Validated using --client-ca-file.

OIDC (Google, Azure AD, Okta, etc.) LDAP/Kerberos via external proxy or webhook. Authentication flow is delegated to provider; API server validates tokens. Important flags: --oidc-issuer-url= --oidc-client-id= --authentication-token-webhook-config-file=

Humans: Administrators (DevOps), developers, SREs via kubectl. Typically use External Identity Providers & TLS Certs. kubeconfig holds the authentication info. Non-Humans: Monitoring, logging, Security, Policy Enforcers, CI/CD, Backup tools. Uses Service Accounts. Bearer tokens are used for authentication.
Provide identities for pods and automation tools. Enable RBAC-based, scoped, auditable access. Avoid misuse of human credentials.

Automatically created per namespace (default SA). Pods inherit the namespace’s default SA unless overridden. Specify a ServiceAccount in pods using: serviceAccountName: <sa-name> Disable token mounting: automountServiceAccountToken: false

Pod starts $\rightarrow$ SA token + CA cert are mounted. Pod connects to API server using HTTPS. Pod validates server certificate via ca.crt. Pod sends JWT token in: Authorization: Bearer <token> API server validates signature using public keys. Request goes through authentication $\rightarrow$ authorization (RBAC). Mounted files: token ca.crt namespace Note: Tokens can be decoded on jwt.io for claims such as sub, iss, aud.

Feature Pre v1.24 v1.24+ Token type Long-lived secret Short-lived projected Stored in Secrets in etcd Not stored; generated per request Expiration None Default 1 hour Rotation None Automatic (internal) Security Weak Strong (audience, TTL)

Manually created by associating a ServiceAccount with a Secret. These tokens never expire, posing security risks. Not recommended due to static nature and security risk.

documents.t: Control Plane Node Inbound: TCP 6443: Kubernetes API Server (Accessed by workers and admin). TCP 2379–2380: etcd server API (Internal Control Plane communication). TCP 5473: Calico Typha (Management proxy for Calico nodes). UDP 4789: Calico VXLAN (Pod-to-Pod communication). Worker Nodes Inbound: TCP 10250: Kubelet API (Used by Control Plane to manage pods). UDP 4789: Calico VXLAN (Pod-to-Pod communication). TCP 30000–32767: NodePort Services (External access to your applications). Common: TCP 22: SSH access for the administrator.

We must disable features that interfere with Kubernetes and enable kernel modules required for container networking. Explanation: Swap: Kubelet’s resource tracking is not designed for swap. If swap is active, performance becomes unpredictable, and the Kubelet will fail to start. Overlay & br_netfilter: overlay is required for the container storage driver. br_netfilter allows the host's bridge to pass traffic to iptables for filtering, which is essential for CNI operation. IP Forwarding: Essential for the node to act as a router and forward traffic from the pod network to other nodes. # Disable Swap sudo swapoff -a sudo sed -i '/ swap / s/^/#/' /etc/fstab # Enable Kernel Modules echo -e "overlay\nbr_netfilter" | sudo tee /etc/modules-load.d/k8s.conf sudo modprobe overlay sudo modprobe br_netfilter # Configure Networking Sysctl cat <<EOF | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/k8s.conf net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables = 1 net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-ip6tables = 1 net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1 EOF sudo sysctl --system
documents.s: Step 1: System Preparation & Kernel Tuning [ALL NODES]

documents.t: Kubernetes uses the Container Runtime Interface (CRI) to run containers. We are using containerd. Explanation: config.toml: This is the primary configuration file for containerd. SystemdCgroup: By default, Kubernetes uses systemd as the cgroup driver. We must tell containerd to use the same driver, or the Kubelet will crash. Sandbox Image: The "Pause" container is a tiny image that holds the network namespace open for every Pod. We pin it to version 3.9 to ensure compatibility with K8s 1.32. # Install containerd sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y containerd # Generate and modify configuration sudo mkdir -p /etc/containerd containerd config default | sudo tee /etc/containerd/config.toml >/dev/null # Set Cgroup driver to systemd sudo sed -i 's/SystemdCgroup = false/SystemdCgroup = true/' /etc/containerd/config.toml # Set the correct sandbox image version sudo sed -i 's#sandbox_image = ".*"#sandbox_image = "registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9"#' /etc/containerd/config.toml # Restart to apply changes sudo systemctl restart containerd

We install the three core binaries: kubeadm (cluster bootstrapper), kubelet (node agent), and kubectl (command-line tool). Explanation: Apt Repository: We use the official pkgs.k8s.io community repository for v1.32. Apt-mark hold: This prevents the packages from being updated automatically. In production, you only upgrade K8s via a controlled, manual process. # Install prerequisites sudo apt-get install -y apt-transport-https ca-certificates curl gpg sudo mkdir -p /etc/apt/keyrings # Add Kubernetes GPG key and Repository curl -fsSL https://pkgs.k8s.io/core:/stable:/v1.32/deb/Release.key | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /etc/apt/keyrings/kubernetes-apt-keyring.gpg echo 'deb [signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/kubernetes-apt-keyring.gpg] https://pkgs.k8s.io/core:/stable:/v1.32/deb/ /' | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/kubernetes.list # Install binaries sudo apt-get update sudo apt-get install -y kubelet kubeadm kubectl sudo apt-mark hold kubelet kubeadm kubectl

This command bootstraps the cluster's internal components (API Server, Scheduler, Controller Manager, and etcd). Explanation: --pod-network-cidr: This defines the internal IP range for Pods. Calico’s default is 192.168.0.0/16. --apiserver-advertise-address: The Private IP of the Control Plane node that workers will use to connect. admin.conf: This file contains the root credentials for your cluster. # Bootstrap the cluster sudo kubeadm init \ --pod-network-cidr=192.168.0.0/16 \ --apiserver-advertise-address=<CONTROL_PLANE_PRIVATE_IP> # Set up local kubeconfig for the user mkdir -p $HOME/.kube sudo cp /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf $HOME/.kube/config sudo chown $(id -u):$(id -g) $HOME/.kube/config

documents.t: The Tigera Operator manages the installation and lifecycle of Calico. Explanation: VXLANCrossSubnet: This tells Calico to use VXLAN (UDP 4789) for traffic that needs to cross subnet boundaries. BGP Disabled: Cloud providers (AWS/Azure) often block BGP. Disabling it avoids "BIRD" errors and forces the cluster to use VXLAN for the overlay. # Install Tigera Operator and CRDs kubectl create -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/projectcalico/calico/v3.30.2/manifests/operator-crds.yaml kubectl create -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/projectcalico/calico/v3.30.2/manifests/tigera-operator.yaml # Apply the network configuration cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f - apiVersion: operator.tigera.io/v1 kind: Installation metadata: name: default spec: calicoNetwork: bgp: Disabled ipPools: - cidr: 192.168.0.0/16 encapsulation: VXLANCrossSubnet EOF

documents.t: To join the data plane nodes to the control plane, generate a join command. # Run this on the Control Plane to get the command kubeadm token create --print-join-command # Run the output of the above command on each Worker Node with 'sudo' # Example: sudo kubeadm join <IP>:6443 --token <token> --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash <hash>

Verify Nodes and Pods: kubectl get nodes kubectl get pods -A Common Issues: Nodes stay "NotReady": Check if Calico pods are running. Usually caused by blocked TCP 5473 (Typha) or UDP 4789 (VXLAN) in your firewall. BIRD Errors in Logs: This happens if BGP is enabled but blocked. Ensure bgp: Disabled was set in the Calico Installation spec. Cgroup Driver Mismatch: If the Kubelet fails to start, check journalctl -u kubelet. If it says "failed to create container: cgroup driver mismatch", revisit Step 2 to ensure SystemdCgroup is set to true in config.toml.

/etc/containerd/config.toml: Runtime settings (SystemdCgroup and Pause image). /etc/sysctl.d/k8s.conf: Kernel settings for networking/routing. /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf: The "Master Key" credentials for cluster administration. $HOME/.kube/config: The local copy of credentials used by kubectl.

Kubernetes follows a strict Semantic Versioning (Major.Minor.Patch). Release Cadence: A new Minor version (e.g., 1.33) is released every 4 months. Support Policy (N-2): Only the 3 most recent minor versions receive security patches. If you are on 1.30 and 1.33 is released, 1.30 becomes End-of-Life (EOL). The "No-Skip" Rule: You cannot skip minor versions (e.g., 1.31 to 1.33). You must upgrade incrementally: 1.31 → 1.32 → 1.33.

To prevent cluster collapse during a rolling upgrade, components must follow these compatibility rules: kube-apiserver: The "anchor." No other component can be newer than the API server. kube-controller-manager / kube-scheduler: Must match the API server version or be at most one minor older. kubelet (Nodes): Can be up to two minors older than the API server. This allows you to upgrade the Control Plane first while workers continue running. kubectl: Supported within +/- 1 minor version of the API server.

Before running any commands: Backup etcd: Use etcdctl snapshot save. Backup Manifests: Copy /etc/kubernetes/ to a safe location. Check CNI/CRI compatibility: Ensure Calico and containerd support the target version. Verify Capacity: Ensure remaining nodes can handle the load when one node is drained.

Step 1: Update the Repository [ALL NODES]​ Kubernetes now uses version-specific repositories. You must point the package manager to the v1.33 path. # Edit the source list sudo vim /etc/apt/sources.list.d/kubernetes.list # Update the line to: # deb [signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/kubernetes-apt-keyring.gpg] https://pkgs.k8s.io/core:/stable:/v1.33/deb/ / sudo apt-get update Step 2: Upgrade the Control Plane [CONTROL PLANE ONLY]​ 1. Upgrade kubeadm binary: unhold allows the package to be updated; hold prevents accidental updates later. sudo apt-mark unhold kubeadm sudo apt-get install -y kubeadm=1.33.4-1.1 sudo apt-mark hold kubeadm 2. Plan the Upgrade: This checks if the cluster is healthy and capable of upgrading. It lists which components will change. sudo kubeadm upgrade plan 3. Apply the Upgrade: This updates the static pod manifests for the API Server, Scheduler, and Controller Manager. It also automatically renews the cluster certificates. sudo kubeadm upgrade apply v1.33.4 4. Upgrade Node Components (Kubelet & Kubectl): The API server is now 1.33, but the local kubelet on the CP node is still 1.32. sudo apt-mark unhold kubelet kubectl sudo apt-get install -y kubelet=1.33.4-1.1 kubectl=1.33.4-1.1 sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl restart kubelet sudo apt-mark hold kubelet kubectl Step 3: Upgrade Worker Nodes [ONE AT A TIME]​ 1. Cordon & Drain (Run from Control Plane): cordon: Marks the node as "SchedulingDisabled." drain: Evicts pods. --ignore-daemonsets is required because DaemonSets are managed by a controller and cannot be "evicted" in the standard way. kubectl cordon worker-1 kubectl drain worker-1 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data 2. Upgrade Node Configuration (Run on Worker Node): First, update the repository as shown in Step 1, then: sudo apt-mark unhold kubeadm kubelet kubectl sudo apt-get update sudo apt-get install -y kubeadm=1.33.4-1.1 # 'upgrade node' retrieves the latest cluster config from the API server sudo kubeadm upgrade node sudo apt-get install -y kubelet=1.33.4-1.1 kubectl=1.33.4-1.1 sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl restart kubelet sudo apt-mark hold kubeadm kubelet kubectl 3. Uncordon (Run from Control Plane): kubectl uncordon worker-1

As seen in the architectural diagram, a PDB limits the number of pods of a replicated application that are down simultaneously from voluntary disruptions (like a drain). Logic: If your app has 4 replicas and a PDB with minAvailable: 3, the drain command will only evict one pod. It will then wait for a replacement to be Ready on another node before evicting the next. The Trap: If your other nodes are full and the replacement pod cannot schedule, the drain command will hang indefinitely. You must add capacity or relax the PDB to proceed.

documents.t: Upgrades can sometimes trigger CNI readiness issues, particularly with BGP/Typha. Symptoms: Nodes show Ready, but pods cannot talk to each other. calico-node logs show "BIRD is not ready." The Fix for Cloud (VXLAN): Most cloud providers don't support BGP. Ensure Calico is told to ignore it: kubectl patch installation.operator.tigera.io default --type=merge -p '{"spec":{"calicoNetwork":{"bgp":"Disabled"}}}' Typha Port: In operator-based installs, calico-node connects to calico-typha. Ensure TCP 5473 is open between all nodes in your Security Groups.

/etc/kubernetes/manifests/: Location of static pods (API Server, etc.). kubeadm upgrade apply modifies these. /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml: The configuration file for the kubelet on that specific node. /etc/apt/sources.list.d/kubernetes.list: The source for your K8s binaries. ~/.kube/config: Your administrative credentials. Always check the server version here vs kubectl get nodes.

Anything created or managed inside a Kubernetes cluster is considered a resource. Examples include pods, deployments, services, and persistent volume claims. Each resource is an object exposed by the Kubernetes API. These resources are organized under API groups, and each group contains multiple versions and kinds of resources. To get a complete list of built-in resources, use: kubectl api-resources

Default Resources: Available by default. Available in both Core (/api) and Named (/apis) groups. Custom Resources: Extends Kubernetes API without core code changes. Created by you or external systems. Available only under named API groups (/apis). Fully compatible with kubectl CLI. Declarative when paired with a controller. Requires a CRD first.

A custom resource is any resource that does not exist in Kubernetes by default but is introduced by the user or an external system to extend the Kubernetes API. Kubernetes exposes resources via its API endpoints: /api — For the core group (e.g., Pods, Services, ConfigMaps). /apis/<group> — For all named groups (e.g., apps/v1 for Deployments). A custom resource becomes part of the /apis path under a new or existing API group. It allows the definition of a specific object kind, schema, and expected behavior.

Created by you or an external system: CRs are user-defined objects created by cluster users or external systems, not built-in Kubernetes components. Exist only under named API groups: CRs live under custom API groups accessed via /apis/{group}; they cannot be part of the core API group (/api). Extend the Kubernetes API without modifying Kubernetes code: CRDs allow the addition of new resource types dynamically without changing or rebuilding the Kubernetes API server. Fully compatible with kubectl: Once a CRD is created, custom resources can be managed using standard kubectl commands (get, describe, create, delete) similar to built-in resources. Declarative when used with controllers: Custom Resources typically represent a desired state. When paired with a controller, the controller ensures the actual cluster state matches this desired state.

A CustomResourceDefinition (CRD) is the mechanism used to inform Kubernetes about the existence of a new resource type. It is a manifest that defines: The API group and version. The singular and plural names of the resource. The resource kind. The OpenAPI validation schema. Once applied, it registers a new resource type in the Kubernetes API server. You can then define and create objects of this new custom kind, which are referred to as Custom Resources (CRs). Note: A Custom Resource (CR) is the object instance, while the CustomResourceDefinition (CRD) is the blueprint or schema that registers that object type with the cluster.

While Custom Resources require a CustomResourceDefinition (CRD), built-in resources (Deployment, Pod, Service) do not use a CRD YAML file. Instead, their definitions are hardcoded into the Kubernetes API server. How to View Built-in Definitions?​ Even though there is no CRD file for built-in resources, you can inspect their schema using the following methods: Kubernetes OpenAPI Schema: The raw schema for all resources: kubectl get --raw /openapi/v2 | jq . kubectl explain: The most user-friendly way to explore built-in resource structures: kubectl explain deployment.spec kubectl explain pod.spec.containers

documents.t: Kubernetes uses the kube-controller-manager as a collection of built-in controllers (e.g., Deployment controller, ReplicaSet controller). These controllers constantly observe the current state of the cluster and compare it against the desired state defined in YAML manifests.
Every controller follows the control loop pattern: Observe desired state $\rightarrow$ Compare with current state $\rightarrow$ Take action to reconcile

A CRD only allows you to store data (configuration). To make that data do something, you need a Custom Controller. The Controller watches the Custom Resource. It compares the .spec (desired state) with the system status. It executes logic (e.g., creating Pods, configuring generic resources, taking backups).
If a resource defines a desired state and can drift from it, it likely needs a controller. If a resource is purely static metadata, no controller is needed.

Apply the following manifest to register the new type: apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1 kind: CustomResourceDefinition metadata: name: backuppolicies.ops.cloudwithvarjosh # Must be <plural>.<group> spec: group: ops.cloudwithvarjosh names: plural: backuppolicies singular: backuppolicy kind: BackupPolicy shortNames: - bp scope: Namespaced versions: - name: v1 served: true storage: true schema: openAPIV3Schema: type: object properties: spec: type: object properties: schedule: type: string description: "Cron schedule for backup." retentionDays: type: integer description: "Days to keep backup." targetPVC: type: string description: "Name of PVC to backup." Once applied, verify with: kubectl get crd backuppolicies.ops.cloudwithvarjosh kubectl api-resources | grep backup Expected output: backuppolicies bp ops.cloudwithvarjosh/v1 true BackupPolicy

Create an instance of the BackupPolicy: apiVersion: ops.cloudwithvarjosh/v1 kind: BackupPolicy metadata: name: mysql-backup namespace: default spec: schedule: "0 1 * * *" retentionDays: 7 targetPVC: mysql-data-pvc Manage this custom resource using standard commands: kubectl get backuppolicies kubectl describe backuppolicy mysql-backup kubectl get backuppolicy mysql-backup -o yaml

For this to function in a production environment, a Custom Controller (usually written in Go or Python) would be running in the cluster. It would: Watch for BackupPolicy objects. Read the schedule and targetPVC. Create Kubernetes CronJob objects dynamically that perform the actual backup work. Update the .status field of the BackupPolicy to reflect the last successful backup time.

As we already know: Custom Resource (CR): A user-defined object that extends Kubernetes functionality (e.g., a BackupPolicy object). It represents the user's intent. Custom Resource Definition (CRD): The schema or blueprint that defines the structure and validation rules of a CR. Custom Controller: A control loop that continuously monitors CRs and reconciles the system's actual state with the desired state defined in the CR.

Definition: Applications that do not store user data or session information locally within the container. State Management: Relies on external systems like distributed caches (e.g., Redis) or databases. Scalability: Highly flexible. Any pod can handle any request. Resilience: Pods are interchangeable; if one fails, traffic is seamlessly routed to another.

Definition: Applications that require internal data storage, persistent identity, or ordered startup (e.g., PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Kafka). Challenges: Data Consistency: Replicas must coordinate to ensure data integrity. Identity: Pods often require stable network identities and persistent storage bindings. Failover: Requires complex logic for leader election and data promotion. Management: Typically utilizes StatefulSets, PersistentVolumeClaims (PVCs), and Headless Services.

Without Operators, managing stateful applications requires extensive coordination between DevOps and Database Administrators (DBAs). DevOps Responsibilities: Provisioning storage (PVCs/StorageClasses). Managing StatefulSets and internal DNS. Configuring RBAC, Secrets, and ServiceAccounts. Scripting health checks (Probes) and backups (CronJobs). DBA Responsibilities: Designing replication topologies (Master-Replica). Managing failover promotion workflows. Tuning performance and handling schema migrations. Ensuring data consistency and replication integrity. The Problem: This manual approach is fragile, labor-intensive, and prone to human error.
A Kubernetes Operator is a design pattern that codifies human operational knowledge into software to automate the management of complex applications.
An Operator acts as a specialist controller running inside the cluster. It automates the entire lifecycle of an application, including installation, upgrades, scaling, backups, and failure recovery.

Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs): Extends the Kubernetes API to include new resource types specific to the application (e.g., KafkaCluster, MySQLReplicaSet). Custom Resources (CRs): Instances of the CRD created by users to declare their desired state (e.g., "Deploy a 3-node cluster"). Custom Controller: The brain of the Operator. It runs a reconciliation loop that watches CRs and interacts with the Kubernetes API to implement logic (scaling, healing, backing up). Kubernetes Resources: The standard objects (Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps) created and managed by the Controller to fulfill the CR's requirements.

The Operator: The overarching pattern containing the logic and definitions. The Controller: Monitors specific CRs. The Action: The Controller reads the CRD, interprets the CR, and creates/updates default Kubernetes resources to match the desired state.

Operator └── Custom Controller ├── Watches: Custom Resources (CRs) ├── Reads: Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) └── May create: Default Kubernetes Resources ├── StatefulSets / Deployments ├── Services / Ingress ├── ConfigMaps / Secrets └── PVCs, CronJobs, Jobs, etc. Operators are not limited to databases. They are a general-purpose automation pattern suitable for any scenario requiring the reconciliation of desired state vs. actual state.
Databases: MySQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB. Monitoring: Prometheus, Thanos. Security: Cert-manager (TLS), Kyverno (Policy). Networking: Istio, Cilium. Backup: Velero.

Operators do not replace Helm or Kustomize; they complement them. Helm/Kustomize: Best for templating and installation (Day 1 operations). Operators: Best for lifecycle management and runtime automation (Day 2+ operations). Combined Workflow: Use Helm to deploy the Operator and its Custom Resources; use the Operator to manage the application's ongoing health and state.
Creating an Operator involves building a controller that watches specific resources.

A basic Operator might simply deploy resources. A mature, production-grade Operator handles: Backup & Restore: Automated scheduling, validation, and disaster recovery. Reliability: Retries, concurrency handling, and self-healing. Observability: Exporting metrics to Prometheus and updating CR status fields. Dynamic Scaling: Adjusting resources based on load or pressure.

Operator SDK (Go): The industry standard for robust, high-performance Operators. Kubebuilder: A scaffolding tool often used within the Operator SDK. Operator SDK (Helm/Ansible): Allows creation of Operators without writing Go code, utilizing existing Charts or Playbooks. Java Operator SDK: For teams integrated into the Java ecosystem. How Do You Choose?​ If you are... Use this... A Go developer Operator SDK (Go) or Kubebuilder Comfortable with Helm Operator SDK (Helm) Strong in Ansible automation Operator SDK (Ansible) Exploring webhooks/lightweight Metacontroller Working in a Java ecosystem Java Operator SDK Note: Go-based Operators (via Operator SDK or Kubebuilder) are the most powerful and widely adopted in production environments.
The demo illustrates the use of the kube-green Operator, designed to reduce CO2 and costs by scaling down non-critical workloads during off-hours.
OLM manages the installation and updates of Operators running in the cluster. Action: Install OLM via the official installation script.
Action: Apply the install manifest from OperatorHub. Result: Creates a Subscription and installs the Operator in the operators namespace.
Check the ClusterServiceVersion (CSV) to ensure the status is Succeeded. Verify the CRD sleepinfos.kube-green.com is registered in the API.

Deploy a standard NGINX Deployment with 2 replicas: # nginx.yaml apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: nginx spec: replicas: 2 selector: matchLabels: app: nginx template: metadata: labels: app: nginx spec: containers: - name: nginx image: nginx

Create a SleepInfo Custom Resource to define the scaling logic: # sleepinfo.yaml apiVersion: kube-green.com/v1alpha1 kind: SleepInfo metadata: labels: app: kube-green name: sleepinfo-sample spec: excludeRef: - apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment name: critical-app sleepAt: '17:55' wakeUpAt: '08:00' weekdays: 0-6 suspendCronJobs: true timeZone: Asia/Kolkata Key Configuration Fields: sleepAt: Time to scale down (e.g., '17:55'). wakeUpAt: Time to restore replicas (e.g., '08:00'). weekdays: Days the policy is active (e.g., 0-6 for Mon-Sun). excludeRef: Specific resources to exempt from the policy (e.g., critical production apps). timeZone: The time zone for the schedule (e.g., 'Asia/Kolkata').
Once the SleepInfo CR is applied, the Operator monitors the time. At sleepAt, the Operator scales target Deployments to 0 replicas. At wakeUpAt, the Operator restores the original replica count.
As applications grow, standard service types like NodePort and LoadBalancer show significant limitations.

Service Type Limitations NodePort Scaling Issues: Managing external traffic to dynamic Node IPs is difficult. Security: Exposing high-range ports (30000-32767) directly on nodes increases the attack surface. LoadBalancer (L4) Layer 4 Only: Operates at TCP/UDP level; cannot route based on HTTP headers, paths, or hostnames. Cost: Each service provisions a dedicated cloud LB (e.g., AWS NLB), leading to high costs. TLS Overhead: Cannot decrypt HTTPS traffic; TLS termination must happen at the Pod level.

Ingress is a Kubernetes API object (a declarative YAML configuration) that acts as a Layer 7 (Application Layer) router. Core Capabilities: Path-based Routing: example.com/api vs example.com/web. Host-based Routing: api.example.com vs web.example.com. TLS/SSL Termination: Handles SSL certificates at the Ingress level so backend apps can receive plain HTTP. Default Backend: A default service can be defined to handle 404s (requests that match no rules). Note: The Ingress resource is just a "Rulebook." It does not perform routing until an Ingress Controller is installed to act as the "Brain."
An Ingress Controller (IC) is a specialized Pod (or set of Pods) that monitors the API Server for Ingress resources and fulfills the rules.

Watch: Monitors API server for new/updated Ingress objects. Translate: Converts YAML rules into LB configuration (e.g., NGINX config or AWS ALB rules). Health Management: Manages health checks for backend services. Routing: Directs traffic to the appropriate Service or Pod IP.

Cloud-Native (e.g., AWS Load Balancer Controller): Provisions a managed cloud LB (ALB) where routing and TLS are handled outside the cluster. 3rd-Party (e.g., NGINX, Traefik, HAProxy): The controller runs inside the cluster as a Pod. A single L4 LoadBalancer/NodePort forwards all traffic to this Pod for internal HTTP routing. Popular Controllers: AWS LBC: Deep integration with EKS, manages ALBs/NLBs. NGINX IC: Most widely used, highly customizable. Contour: Built on Envoy, optimized for multi-team ingress. Istio Ingress Gateway: Part of the service mesh; enables mTLS and fine-grained traffic management.
Objective: Use a single AWS Application Load Balancer (ALB) to distribute traffic to multiple backend services based on the URL context path.

Using eksctl ensures reproducibility. Note the withOIDC: true field; this is mandatory for the ALB Controller to have permission to create AWS resources via IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts). eks-config.yaml: apiVersion: eksctl.io/v1alpha5 kind: ClusterConfig metadata: name: cwvj-ingress-demo region: us-east-2 managedNodeGroups: - name: cwvj-eks-priv-ng instanceType: t3.small desiredCapacity: 4 privateNetworking: true iam: withOIDC: true Apply: eksctl create cluster -f eks-config.yaml

IAM Policy: Download and create the policy that allows the controller to manage ALBs. curl -O https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes-sigs/aws-load-balancer-controller/v2.13.3/docs/install/iam_policy.json aws iam create-policy --policy-name AWSLoadBalancerControllerIAMPolicy --policy-document file://iam_policy.json Service Account (IRSA): Create the SA and associate it with the IAM policy. eksctl create iamserviceaccount \ --cluster=cwvj-ingress-demo \ --namespace=kube-system \ --name=aws-load-balancer-controller \ --attach-policy-arn=arn:aws:iam::<ACCOUNT_ID>:policy/AWSLoadBalancerControllerIAMPolicy \ --approve Install via Helm: helm repo add eks https://aws.github.io/eks-charts helm install aws-load-balancer-controller eks/aws-load-balancer-controller \ -n kube-system \ --set clusterName=cwvj-ingress-demo \ --set serviceAccount.create=false \ --set serviceAccount.name=aws-load-balancer-controller
