documents.t: Deploy apps with topologySpreadConstraints to ensure High Availability across Availability Zones (AZs). Microservice snippet (iPhone-app): spec: topologySpreadConstraints: - maxSkew: 1 topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway labelSelector: matchLabels: app: iphone-page

The Ingress manifest tells the LBC to build the AWS ALB. 05-ingress.yaml: apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: Ingress metadata: name: ingress-demo1 namespace: app1-ns annotations: alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/scheme: internet-facing alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/target-type: ip # Direct Pod routing alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/listen-ports: '[{"HTTP": 80}]' spec: ingressClassName: alb # Vital: Connects this resource to AWS LBC rules: - http: paths: - path: /iphone pathType: Prefix backend: service: name: iphone-svc port: number: 80 - path: /android pathType: Prefix backend: service: name: android-svc port: number: 80 - path: / pathType: Prefix backend: service: name: desktop-svc port: number: 80
This is a critical performance setting in AWS EKS.

How it works: The ALB registers individual Pod IPs as targets. Requirement: Requires AWS VPC CNI (default in EKS) which assigns VPC-routable IPs to pods. Benefit: Bypasses NodePort and kube-proxy hops. Fewer hops = lower latency. Flow: User -> ALB -> Pod IP.

How it works: The ALB registers EC2 Worker Nodes as targets. Mechanism: Traffic hits a NodePort on the EC2 instance, is handled by kube-proxy, then routed to a Pod (potentially on a different node). Drawback: Adds network latency and "double-hopping." Flow: User -> ALB -> NodePort -> kube-proxy -> Pod IP.

Kubernetes: kubectl describe ingress ingress-demo1 -n app1-ns. Check the "Address" field for the ALB DNS. AWS Console: Navigate to EC2 > Load Balancers. Ensure the state is Active and Target Groups are Healthy. URL Test: http://<ALB-DNS>/iphone -> iPhone Service http://<ALB-DNS>/android -> Android Service http://<ALB-DNS>/ -> Default Desktop Service

To avoid orphaned resources and residual costs: Delete Ingress first: kubectl delete ingress ingress-demo1 -n app1-ns. (This allows the LBC to clean up the AWS ALB, Security Groups, and Target Groups). Delete Cluster: eksctl delete cluster --name cwvj-ingress-demo.

Host-Based Routing: Traffic is directed to different backend services based on the Host header of the HTTP request (e.g., iphone.cwvj.click vs. android.cwvj.click). TLS Termination: The Application Load Balancer (ALB) handles the heavy lifting of decrypting HTTPS traffic using an SSL certificate. This offloads the CPU burden from your Pods, allowing them to receive plain HTTP traffic. ACM (AWS Certificate Manager): A service that lets you easily provision, manage, and deploy public and private SSL/TLS certificates.

To ensure browsers do not show "Not Secure" warnings, you must prove domain ownership. Request Certificate: Go to ACM and request a Public Certificate. Apex vs. Wildcard: A Wildcard cert (*.cwvj.click) covers subdomains but not the apex domain (cwvj.click). Best Practice: Request a single certificate and add both cwvj.click and *.cwvj.click to it for full coverage. DNS Validation: ACM will provide CNAME records. Click the "Create records in Route 53" button to automate the validation process.

The Ingress Controller reads annotations to configure the ALB for HTTPS. 05-ingress.yaml: apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: Ingress metadata: name: ingress-demo2 namespace: app1-ns annotations: # ALB Configuration alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/scheme: internet-facing alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/target-type: ip alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/load-balancer-name: cwvj-ingress-demo2 # SSL/TLS Settings alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/certificate-arn: arn:aws:acm:us-east-2:123456789:certificate/uuid alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/listen-ports: '[{"HTTP": 80}, {"HTTPS": 443}]' alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: '443' # Auto-redirect HTTP to HTTPS # Health Check (Must match app path) alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/healthcheck-protocol: HTTP alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/healthcheck-port: traffic-port alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/healthcheck-path: /index.html alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/success-codes: '200' spec: ingressClassName: alb rules: - http: paths: - path: /iphone pathType: Prefix backend: service: name: iphone-svc port: number: 80

Once the Ingress creates the ALB, it will have a long DNS name (e.g., k8s-default-xxxx.us-east-2.elb.amazonaws.com). You must map your custom domain to it. Go to Route 53 > Hosted Zones > yourdomain.com. Create a Record. Toggle Alias: Yes. Route traffic to: Alias to Application and Classic Load Balancer. Select your Region and choose the ALB DNS name generated by the Ingress.
This is the standard for hosting multiple distinct applications (e.g., iphone.domain.com and android.domain.com) behind a single entry point.
In host-based routing, each subdomain usually serves from the root / path. You must ensure your applications serve their content (like index.html) from the root directory rather than a nested folder.

Instead of one host with multiple paths, we define multiple hosts. 06-host-ingress.yaml: apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: Ingress metadata: name: ingress-host-demo namespace: app1-ns annotations: alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/scheme: internet-facing alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/target-type: ip alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/certificate-arn: arn:aws:acm:us-east-2:123456789:certificate/uuid alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/listen-ports: '[{"HTTPS": 443}]' spec: ingressClassName: alb rules: - host: iphone.cwvj.click http: paths: - path: / pathType: Prefix backend: service: name: iphone-svc port: number: 80 - host: android.cwvj.click http: paths: - path: / pathType: Prefix backend: service: name: android-svc port: number: 80 - host: cwvj.click # Apex domain http: paths: - path: / pathType: Prefix backend: service: name: desktop-svc port: number: 80

Browser Padlock: Click the padlock in the browser; verify the certificate is issued by "Amazon" and matches your domain. HTTPS Redirection: Enter http://cwvj.click and verify it automatically switches to https://. ALB Listener Rules: Go to AWS Console > EC2 > Load Balancers > Listeners > HTTPS:443 > Rules. You should see rules mapping Host: iphone.cwvj.click to the specific Target Group. DNS Propagation: Use dig iphone.cwvj.click to ensure it resolves to the ALB's IPs.

Type Logic Use Case Path-Based domain.com/app1, domain.com/app2 Microservices sharing a single domain. Host-Based app1.domain.com, app2.domain.com Multi-tenancy or distinct product lines. TLS/SSL https:// via ALB Annotations Secure production traffic & compliance.

To avoid residual AWS costs, always delete resources in this specific order: Delete Ingress: kubectl delete ingress <name>. This triggers the controller to delete the ALB, Security Groups, and Target Groups in AWS. Delete ACM Certs: Delete certificates only after the ALB is gone. Delete Route 53 Records: Remove Alias A-records. Delete Cluster: Finally, run eksctl delete cluster --name <name>.

The Kubernetes Gateway API is a SIG-Network project designed to evolve and eventually replace the Ingress API. It provides a more expressive, extensible, and role-oriented model for managing networking in a cluster.
documents.s: Kubernetes Gateway API: The Modern Evolution of Ingress

documents.t: Before the Gateway API, Ingress was the standard, but it suffered from several architectural flaws: Minimal Specification: Native Ingress only supports basic HTTP/S host and path routing. Annotation Overload: Advanced features like rate limiting, timeouts, retries, and canary splits were never standardized. They were implemented via vendor-specific annotations (e.g., nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/...). Lack of Validation: The API server does not validate annotations. Typos lead to silent failures. Vendor Lock-in: Annotations are not portable. Switching from NGINX to AWS ALB requires a complete manifest rewrite. Namespace Constraints: Ingress resources are confined to a single namespace. Sharing one Load Balancer across multiple namespaces is difficult and relies on non-standard controller hacks. RBAC Weakness: There is no native way to delegate control of specific paths or hosts to different teams within a single Ingress resource.
documents.s: 1. Why Evolve? Issues with Existing Ingress

documents.t: The Gateway API introduces a resource model that separates infrastructure management from application routing, aligning with three distinct organizational roles:

Scope: Cluster-scoped. Role: Acts as a blueprint for Gateway implementations. Function: Defines the controller responsible for the class (e.g., nginx.org/gateway-controller). It is analogous to a StorageClass.

Scope: Namespace-scoped. Role: Provisions the actual networking infrastructure (Cloud LB or In-cluster proxy). Function: Defines Listeners (port, protocol, hostname) and TLS settings. It serves as the entry point for traffic.
Scope: Namespace-scoped. Role: Defines the logic for how traffic is directed to backend Services. Resources: HTTPRoute, GRPCRoute, TCPRoute, UDPRoute. Logic: Routes attach to Gateways via parentRefs.

Gateway API moves features that previously required annotations directly into the core API spec: Traffic Splitting: Native support for weight-based routing (Canary and Blue-Green deployments). Request/Response Filtering: Built-in ability to modify headers, perform redirects, or rewrite paths. Cross-Namespace Routing: Gateways can attach routes from different namespaces. ReferenceGrant: A security resource that explicitly allows a Route in Namespace A to reference a Service in Namespace B, preventing unauthorized cross-namespace traffic hijacking.

A specific KIND configuration is required to map a hostPort to a containerPort, allowing local access to the NodePort service. 00-kind-cluster.yaml: kind: Cluster apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4 nodes: - role: control-plane extraPortMappings: - containerPort: 31000 hostPort: 31000 # Map local 31000 to cluster 31000 Apply: kind create cluster --name=gateway-api --config=00-kind-cluster.yaml

As applications grow, the number of Kubernetes resources increases rapidly. Helm acts as a full application lifecycle manager for Kubernetes.

Injecting dynamic values (image tags, ports). Tracking deployments across environments. Applying upgrades without breaking workloads. Rolling back when issues occur. Packaging and distributing applications.

Feature Kustomize Helm Configuration Management Patches and overlays Go templates with conditionals and loops Versioned Packaging No Yes Release Tracking No Yes Rollback Support No Yes Distribution No Chart repositories Lifecycle Management No Install, upgrade, delete operations Hooks and Tests No Yes Kustomize handles configuration overlays but doesn't support: Versioning or packaging. Rollbacks or release tracking. Distribution to other teams. Dynamic templating. Hooks, tests, or lifecycle events.

Kustomize is a native Kubernetes configuration management tool for environment-specific customization without templating. It uses a declarative base + overlays approach.

Multiple Environments: (dev, staging, prod) need slightly different configs. Manual Duplication: Copy-pasting YAML causes errors and "config drift." Complexity: A single application across 3 tiers and 3 environments can result in ~45 objects to manage manually.

Base: Common configuration shared across all environments (standard YAML). Overlays: Environment-specific customizations that "patch" the base. No Templating: Pure YAML with declarative patches (unlike Helm’s Go templates). Native: Bundled with kubectl (v1.14+).

Feature Kustomize Helm Native to K8s Yes (built into kubectl) No (separate binary) Templating No Yes (Go templates) Variables No Yes (values.yaml) Complexity Low Medium-High Package Management No Yes (Charts) Logic/Loops No Yes Use Case Simple to medium apps Medium to complex apps
Bundled: Part of kubectl since v1.14. Use kubectl apply -k. Standalone: curl -s "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes-sigs/kustomize/master/hack/install_kustomize.sh" | bash
Critical Rule: The file must be named exactly kustomization.yaml (all lowercase). Kustomization.yaml or kustomization.yml will not work.

kustomize-demo/ ├── base/ │ ├── deployment.yaml │ ├── service.yaml │ └── kustomization.yaml └── overlays/ ├── dev/ │ └── kustomization.yaml ├── staging/ │ └── kustomization.yaml └── prod/ └── kustomization.yaml
Lists raw Kubernetes YAML files with no environment-specific customizations. apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1 kind: Kustomization resources: - deploy.yaml - svc.yaml
References the base via a relative path and applies customizations. apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1 kind: Kustomization resources: - ../../base nameSuffix: -dev
Built-in mechanisms to modify resources declaratively without editing raw YAML.

namePrefix / nameSuffix: Add prefixes/suffixes to all resource names. namespace: Assign a specific namespace to all resources. images: Override container image names or tags. replicas: Change replica count for specific deployments. labels: Add labels to metadata and selectors. includeSelectors: true ensures consistency. commonAnnotations: Add annotations to all resources.

Transformers cannot modify: Arbitrary nested fields in container specs. Specific containerPort values. Environment variables (limited support). Volume mounts or probes. Deeply nested fields beyond exposed transformers.
Precise, field-level modifications for deeply nested fields not supported by transformers.
add: Add new field/array entry. replace: Replace value (field must exist). remove: Delete field/element. copy: Copy value between paths. move: Move value between paths.
Method Format Status patches (generic) YAML/JSON inline Preferred patchesJson6902 JSON patch file Deprecated patchesStrategicMerge YAML file Deprecated

Base Files: deploy.yaml (name: nginx-deploy), svc.yaml (name: nginx-svc). Base kustomization.yaml: apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1 kind: Kustomization resources: - deploy.yaml - svc.yaml Dev Overlay kustomization.yaml: apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1 kind: Kustomization resources: - ../../base nameSuffix: -dev Note: ../../base means go up two levels, then into base/.

Dev Overlay kustomization.yaml: apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1 kind: Kustomization resources: - ../../base namePrefix: app1- nameSuffix: -dev namespace: dev labels: - pairs: env: dev includeSelectors: true commonAnnotations: branch: dev support: 800-800-700 images: - name: nginx newName: nginx newTag: "latest" replicas: - name: nginx-deploy count: 2

Inline patching in kustomization.yaml is the most flexible approach (best for Kustomize v5+). patches: - target: group: apps version: v1 kind: Deployment name: nginx-deploy patch: |- - op: add path: /spec/template/spec/containers/0/env value: - name: LOG_LEVEL value: debug - op: replace path: /spec/template/spec/containers/0/resources value: requests: cpu: "100m" memory: "128Mi" limits: cpu: "500m" memory: "256Mi" - op: remove path: /metadata/labels/unused - target: version: v1 kind: Service name: nginx-svc patch: |- - op: replace path: /spec/ports/0/nodePort value: 31000
add: Injects LOG_LEVEL=debug to the container. replace: Overwrites the resources block and hardcodes a nodePort. remove: Deletes an unused metadata label.
Critical: Commands must run in a directory containing a kustomization.yaml or reference that directory.
kubectl kustomize base kubectl kustomize overlays/dev kubectl kustomize overlays/stage

# Create namespaces first kubectl create namespace dev kubectl create namespace stage kubectl create namespace prod # Apply using -k (Kustomize directory) kubectl apply -k overlays/dev kubectl apply -k overlays/stage kubectl apply -k overlays/prod Note: -k is for Kustomize directories; -f is for standard files.

Deprecated: patchesJson6902 and patchesStrategicMerge. Why: Brittle with custom resources, lacks flexibility compared to the unified patches field. Migration: From the overlay directory, run: kustomize edit fix This auto-converts deprecated sections to the modern patches format.

Replace vs Add: Using replace for a field that doesn't exist yet (must use add). Path Syntax: Using incorrect path syntax for nested fields (use / for nesting). Missing File: Forgetting to include a kustomization.yaml in a directory. CLI Flags: Using -f instead of -k during kubectl apply. Relative Paths: Providing incorrect relative paths to the base in overlays. Naming: Naming the file Kustomization.yaml or kustomization.yml (Must be lowercase .yaml).

StatefulSets are the workload API object used to manage stateful applications. While Deployments are designed for stateless microservices, StatefulSets provide the necessary guarantees for applications requiring a unique identity, persistent data, and a specific deployment order.

Stateless Applications: These are "just code." Every instance is identical and interchangeable. They do not store data locally that needs to survive a restart. Examples: Nginx, standard web APIs. Management: Managed via Deployments. Stateful Applications: These are "code + data." Their behavior depends on previous interactions or stored data. If a stateful pod restarts, it must reconnect to the exact same data volume and retain its unique identity. Examples: Databases (MySQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB), Distributed Systems (Kafka, Elasticsearch, Zookeeper). Management: Managed via StatefulSets.

In a traditional 3-tier architecture, state management is a major challenge: Web Tier (Frontend): Can become "accidental stateful" if user sessions (login status, shopping carts) are stored in local RAM. If a pod crashes, the session is lost, and the user is logged out. Application Tier (Backend): Usually stateless, handling logic and DB communication. Data Tier (Database): Inherently stateful; the source of truth. Modern Solution: Externalizing State To improve scalability, state is moved to systems like Amazon ElastiCache (Redis). This allows any frontend/backend pod to fetch session data from a centralized cache, making the application tiers truly stateless and easier to scale.
A production database cluster usually consists of one Primary node (handles writes) and multiple Replicas (handle reads).

Initial Cloning: A new replica must first copy the existing dataset (e.g., 100GB). To avoid overwhelming the Primary, a Cascading Clone is used (Replica-2 clones from Replica-1). Continuous Replication: Once cloned, the replica syncs live changes via a stream (Binlogs or WAL). Most systems use a Star Topology for live sync, where all replicas connect directly to the Primary.

Deployments are unsuitable for stateful workloads because: Random Naming: Deployments use random hashes (e.g., db-x8j2k). Stateful apps need predictable names (e.g., mysql-0). Lack of Pod-Level DNS: You cannot target a specific pod in a Deployment via a stable DNS name. Unordered Rollouts: Deployments may start/stop all pods at once, potentially breaking a database Quorum or Primary election. Generic Storage: Deployments struggle to ensure Pod A always gets its specific Volume A back after a restart or reschedule. What happens if a pod crashes in a Deployment? If replica-1 crashes and is rescheduled as replica-4, the Primary DB will consider it a new, unauthorized node and refuse to replicate data to it. Databases rely on fixed identifiers (Hostnames, Server IDs, or Replication Slots).

StatefulSets provide the "Sticky Identity" required for stateful applications: Feature Deployment StatefulSet Pod Names Random (e.g., web-5f69b) Deterministic (e.g., web-0, web-1) Network ID Service IP (Shared) Individual Pod DNS (via Headless Service) Startup/Shutdown Parallel / Non-deterministic Ordered (Sequential 0 to N / N to 0) Storage Mapping Shared or ephemeral 1:1 Pod-to-Volume "Sticky" mapping Use Case Stateless APIs, Frontends Databases, Kafka, Zookeeper

Headless Service: Required to create DNS records for each pod. It is defined by setting clusterIP: None. DNS Format: <pod-name>.<service-name>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local volumeClaimTemplates: Instead of sharing one PVC, this field automates the creation of a unique PVC for every pod in the StatefulSet. Update Strategy - Partition (Advanced): StatefulSets allow "Partitioned" updates, where only pods with an ordinal greater than or equal to the partition are updated. This allows for canary-style updates of stateful clusters.

Block Storage (EBS): Preferred for databases due to low latency and high IOPS. Access Modes: RWO / RWOP (ReadWriteOnce / ReadWriteOncePod): Ensures only one pod can write to the disk at a time, preventing data corruption. ACID Properties: Databases prioritize Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability. Block storage ensures that once data is written, it survives power failures. CAP Theorem: StatefulSets help manage Consistency and Availability by maintaining stable nodes during network partitions.

Use volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer to ensure the EBS volume is created in the same Availability Zone (AZ) where the pod is scheduled. apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1 kind: StorageClass metadata: name: ebs-sc-gp3 annotations: storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true" provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com parameters: type: gp3 volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer reclaimPolicy: Delete allowVolumeExpansion: true
kubectl create ns mysql-ha
apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: mysql namespace: mysql-ha spec: clusterIP: None # Required for Headless selector: app: mysql ports: - port: 3306

This includes pod anti-affinity to ensure pods are spread across different nodes/AZs. apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: StatefulSet metadata: name: mysql namespace: mysql-ha spec: serviceName: mysql replicas: 3 selector: matchLabels: app: mysql template: metadata: labels: app: mysql spec: terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 10 affinity: podAntiAffinity: requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution: - labelSelector: matchLabels: app: mysql topologyKey: "kubernetes.io/hostname" containers: - name: mysql image: mysql:8.0 ports: - containerPort: 3306 env: - name: MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD value: "password123" volumeMounts: - name: mysql-data mountPath: /var/lib/mysql volumeClaimTemplates: - metadata: name: mysql-data spec: accessModes: ["ReadWriteOncePod"] storageClassName: ebs-sc-gp3 resources: requests: storage: 5Gi
kubectl get pods -o wide # Verify sequential creation (mysql-0, then mysql-1...) kubectl get pvc # Verify unique PVC for each pod
kubectl get pods -o wide --show-labels
kubectl exec -it mysql-1 -- bash cd /var/lib/mysql echo "Persistence Test: CloudWithVarJosh" > persistence_check.txt exit
Identify the node hosting mysql-1 and terminate the EC2 instance in the AWS Console. # Get node name kubectl get pod mysql-1 -o jsonpath='{.spec.nodeName}'
kubectl get pods -w The pod will move from Unknown/Terminating $\rightarrow$ Pending $\rightarrow$ ContainerCreating. Kubernetes detects the failure and recreates the pod.
Once the pod is Running, exec back in: kubectl exec -it mysql-1 -- cat /var/lib/mysql/persistence_check.txt
The "Age" of the PVC will be much older than the "Age" of the new Pod, confirming the volume was reattached, not recreated. kubectl get pvc mysql-data-mysql-1

Prediction: Pods are named [name]-[ordinal]. Ordering: Deployment is $0 \to (N-1)$. Termination is $(N-1) \to 0$. Headless Service: Must match the serviceName field in the StatefulSet spec. Storage: volumeClaimTemplates creates PVCs that persist even if the StatefulSet is deleted (manual cleanup required for safety). Network Identity: Pods are reachable via pod-name.service-name.
Linux is an open-source OS Kernel. It is not a full Operating System by itself; it is the "engine" that manages communication between software and hardware.

1969 (UNIX): Created at Bell Labs. It was proprietary and expensive. 1983 (GNU Project): Richard Stallman founded the Free Software Foundation. He aimed to build a free UNIX-like OS. He created the "Userland" tools (Compiler, Shell, Editor). 1987 (Minix): A small UNIX-like system created for education. 1991 (Linux): Linus Torvalds created the Linux Kernel as a personal project because he wanted a free version of Minix. GNU/Linux: What we call "Linux" today is actually the GNU tools running on top of the Linux Kernel.

Layer Role Description Kernel Resource Manager Manages CPU, RAM, Disk, and Hardware Drivers. Shell Command Interpreter A program (like Bash or Zsh) that takes user input and passes it to the Kernel. Userland Application Space Where user applications (Browsers, Web Servers, Editors) run.

Understanding this is critical for troubleshooting system-level failures. BIOS/UEFI: The first code to run. It performs POST (Power On Self Test) to verify hardware like RAM and Keyboard. MBR/GPT (Bootloader Search): The system looks for the bootable device (Disk). Bootloader (GRUB2): A small program on the disk that allows you to select the OS. It loads the Kernel into memory (RAM). Kernel Initialization: The kernel starts hardware drivers and mounts the root filesystem (/). Init Process (PID 1): The kernel starts the very first process in userspace.

The Init Process always has Process ID 1. It is the parent of all other processes. Spawning: Every application you run is a "Child" of the process that started it. Adopting Orphans: If a parent process dies unexpectedly, PID 1 "adopts" the children to ensure they are monitored and eventually cleaned up. Zombie Processes: What it is: A process that has finished execution but still has an entry in the Process Table. The Cause: The parent process failed to call the wait() system call to collect the exit status. The Danger: Zombies don't use RAM, but they consume PIDs. If you reach the system's PID limit, you cannot start any new processes (including ls or ssh). The Fix: You cannot "kill" a zombie because it is already dead. You must kill/restart the Parent process.

Logic: Uses Runlevels (0: Halt, 1: Single User, 3: Multi-user CLI, 5: GUI, 6: Reboot). Execution: Sequential. It starts Service A, waits for it to finish, then starts Service B. This makes booting very slow.

Logic: Uses Target Units (e.g., multi-user.target). Execution: Parallel. It starts multiple services at once, resulting in significantly faster boot times. Naming: Background processes are called Daemons (ending in "d", e.g., systemd, sshd, dockerd). Runlevel Systemd Target Description 0 poweroff.target Shuts down the system. 1 rescue.target Single-user mode (Maintenance). 3 multi-user.target Multi-user mode, CLI only (Standard for Servers). 5 graphical.target Multi-user mode with GUI. 6 reboot.target Reboots the system.

Command Purpose systemctl start <svc> Start a service (current session only). systemctl stop <svc> Stop a service. systemctl restart <svc> Stop and then start. systemctl enable <svc> Configure service to start automatically on boot (creates a symlink). systemctl disable <svc> Stop service from starting on boot. systemctl status <svc> View active state, Main PID, and recent logs. systemctl is-enabled <svc> Check if it will start on next boot.

The APT (Advanced Package Tool) manages software. sudo apt update: Refreshes the local repository index (the list of what is available). sudo apt install <name> -y: Downloads and installs. sudo apt remove <name>: Deletes the package but keeps config files. sudo apt purge <name>: Deletes the package AND config files.
Linux is a multi-user system where every process and file is owned by a specific identity. Identity is defined by UID (User ID) and GID (Group ID).

This file is world-readable and contains the basic attributes of every user on the system. Format: username:password_placeholder:UID:GID:GECOS:home_directory:shell Field Description Username Unique login name (e.g., root, vboxuser). Password Usually an x, indicating the actual hashed password is in /etc/shadow. UID 0: Root. 1-999: System users (daemons/services). 1000+: Human users. GID The primary group ID for this user. GECOS General info/Comments (often the user's full name). Home Dir Path to user's home (e.g., /home/alice). Shell Default CLI (e.g., /bin/bash). Service accounts often use /usr/sbin/nologin.

Only readable by root. It stores hashed passwords and aging metadata. Format: username:hash:lastchange:min:max:warn:inactive:expire:reserved Field Meaning Username Must match the entry in /etc/passwd. Hashed Password Starts with $id$. $1$=MD5, $5$=SHA-256, $6$=SHA-512 (Modern default). Last Change Days since Jan 1, 1970 (Unix Epoch) that the password was last changed. Min Days Minimum days required before the user is allowed to change password again. Max Days Number of days before the password must be changed. Warn Days Days before expiration to start showing a warning message at login. Inactive Days after password expires before the account is totally disabled. Expire Absolute date (days since epoch) when the account will be disabled.

id <user>: Displays UID, Primary GID, and all secondary groups. whoami: Returns the effective username of the current session. useradd -m <user>: Creates a new user and generates a home directory. usermod -aG <group> <user>: Adds a user to a supplementary group. Warning: Always use -a (append). Without it, the user is removed from all other groups. userdel -r <user>: Deletes user and removes their home directory.
Groups allow you to apply the same permissions to multiple users at once. Source File: /etc/group $\rightarrow$ groupname:password:GID:user_list
groupadd <name>: Create a new group. groupadd -g 2000 <name>: Create a group with a specific GID. groups <user>: List all groups a specific user belongs to. groupdel <name>: Delete a group.
Run ls -l to view permissions. The first 10 characters define the access level.

Position 1: Type (-=File, d=Directory, l=Link). Positions 2-4 (Owner): Permissions for the user who owns the file. Positions 5-7 (Group): Permissions for users in the file's group. Positions 8-10 (Others): Permissions for everyone else on the system.

Value Symbolic Meaning 4 r-- Read: View contents (File) or List files (Dir). 2 -w- Write: Modify contents (File) or Create/Delete files (Dir). 1 --x Execute: Run as program (File) or Enter/CD into (Dir). Common Masks: 755 (rwxr-xr-x): Standard for scripts/directories. 644 (rw-r--r--): Standard for configuration files. 600 (rw-------): Private files (like SSH keys).

Used when standard rwx is insufficient for system operations. SUID (Set User ID) - u+s: Effect: The file runs with the privileges of the File Owner, not the user running it. Visual: rwsr-xr-x. If the 's' is capital (S), the execute bit is missing. Example: /usr/bin/passwd (allows users to write to /etc/shadow). SGID (Set Group ID) - g+s: On Files: Runs with group privileges. On Directories: Any new files created inside inherit the parent directory’s group. Use Case: Collaborative folders where everyone needs to work on the same group files. Sticky Bit - +t: Effect: Only the Owner of a file (or Root) can delete or rename it, even if others have write access to the directory. Visual: rwxrwxrwt. Example: /tmp directory.

chown <user> <file>: Change the individual owner. chown <user>:<group> <file>: Change both owner and group at once. chgrp <group> <file>: Change the group ownership only. -R flag: Use with chown/chmod to apply changes recursively to all files inside a directory.
The sudo (SuperUser Do) command allows a user to run programs with the security privileges of another user (usually root).

sudo visudo: Always use this command to edit sudoers. It locks the file and performs a syntax check. A single typo in this file can break your system's root access. Syntax: user host=(runas_user:runas_group) commands %admin ALL=(ALL) ALL $\rightarrow$ Members of group admin have full sudo. alice ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/apt $\rightarrow$ Alice can run apt without a password.
sudo -i: Opens a persistent root login shell. sudo !!: Re-runs the last command entered with sudo (very common in workflows).

Permission On a File On a Directory Read (r) Read file content (cat, vi). List files inside (ls). Write (w) Edit/Change file contents. Add, delete, or rename files inside. Execute (x) Run the file as a script/binary. cd into the directory or access sub-files.
Kubernetes uses DNS for service discovery and communication between components. CoreDNS is the default DNS provider since Kubernetes v1.13, replacing the legacy kube-dns implementation.

Deployment: Runs in the kube-system namespace with 2+ replicas. Service: kube-dns ClusterIP service (port 53). Ports: 53/UDP, 53/TCP: DNS resolution. 9153/TCP: Prometheus metrics (request counts, latency, cache stats).

The Domain Name System (DNS) is a hierarchical and distributed naming system that maps human-readable domain names to machine-readable IP addresses.

Hierarchical: Follows a strict tree-like structure. Distributed: Spread across the globe for massive scalability. Cached: Heavily used at multiple levels to improve performance. Delegated: Responsibility is handed off to avoid central bottlenecks. Beyond name resolution, DNS supports: Load balancing Failover mechanisms Service separation via subdomains

Part Description . Root — The starting point of the DNS hierarchy. resolvers always assume this. io TLD (Top-Level Domain) — Represents a category (e.g., .com, .edu, .io). kubernetes Second-Level Domain — Registered under the .io TLD. www Subdomain — A prefix to the main domain used for specific services (web, mail, etc.). Note on "www": In DNS, "www" is just another subdomain with no special intrinsic meaning. Any behavior (like redirection) must be explicitly configured. DNS maps it via CNAME or A records, but HTTP-level redirection occurs at the web server or CDN.
The DNS lookup flow moves from Top to Bottom through four high-level stages:
documents.s: WHAT HAPPENS WHEN WE TYPE A DOMAIN NAME?

documents.t: The OS checks its local DNS cache. If not found, the query is forwarded to a Recursive Resolver (usually provided by your ISP or public services like Google 8.8.8.8).

If the record isn't in the resolver's cache, it initiates a series of queries: Query Root Nameserver: Asks "Who handles .io?" Query TLD Nameserver: Asks "Who handles kubernetes.io?" Query Authoritative Nameserver: Asks "What is the IP for docs.kubernetes.io?" Receive final IP address.
The resolver caches the result based on its TTL (Time to Live) value and returns the IP to the client system.
The browser uses the IP address to establish a TCP connection, performs a TLS handshake, and sends HTTP requests.

View DNS configuration (macOS): scutil --dns Manually inspect resolution: dig docs.kubernetes.io The SERVER field in the output indicates which resolver handled the query. Strategy Tip: During infrastructure changes, reduce the TTL well in advance so that updates propagate quickly, then restore the original TTL after the move is complete.

A DNS namespace is too large for one authority. It is divided into DNS Zones, each managed by a specific authority. DNS Zone: A record set for a portion of the DNS hierarchy. DNS Zone File: A database containing all records required to resolve names within that zone.
SOA (Start of Authority): Defines authority, primary server, and refresh timers. NS (Nameserver): Defines which servers are authoritative for the zone.

Record Description A Maps a domain to an IPv4 address. AAAA Maps a domain to an IPv6 address. CNAME Canonical Name — Points one domain name to another (Alias). MX Mail Exchange — Specifies mail servers. Points to hostnames, never IPs. TXT Provides arbitrary text (often used for SPF, DKIM, or verification). NS Authoritative nameservers for the domain.

Non-Authoritative Nameservers: Run by ISPs or public providers (Google, Cloudflare). They do not store original records; they speed up queries via caching. Authoritative Nameservers: Provide original, accurate answers for specific zones. They serve zone data directly and do not perform recursive lookups for other domains.

Domain Registry: The "Wholesaler." Manages all names under a specific TLD. (e.g., Verisign manages .com). Domain Registrar: The "Retailer." Allows users to buy and renew names. (e.g., GoDaddy, Namecheap). Crucial Note: Domain registration and DNS hosting are independent. A registrar manages ownership, while a DNS host (like Route53 or Cloudflare) manages the actual zone files and records.

The root domain is the starting point of the DNS hierarchy. There are 13 logical root nameservers operated by 12 organizations. The zone file is maintained by IANA and distributed by Verisign. Root servers use Anycast routing, meaning there are actually hundreds of physical instances worldwide for high availability.

Client requests cwvj.io. Local Cache check. ISP/Public Resolver takes the query. Resolver asks Root: "Who handles .io?" Root returns Authoritative NS for .io. Resolver asks .io TLD NS: "Who handles cwvj.io?" TLD NS returns Authoritative NS for cwvj.io. Resolver asks Authoritative NS: "What is the IP for cwvj.io?" Authoritative NS returns the A record. Resolver caches and returns IP to Client. Client establishes connection.

Kubernetes NetworkPolicies are Layer 3 (IP-based) and Layer 4 (Port-based) security rules. They act as a distributed firewall for your pods, allowing you to control traffic flow at a granular level. By default, Kubernetes operates on an "Allow All" model (non-isolated). NetworkPolicies allow you to transition to a "Zero-Trust" model where only explicitly defined traffic is permitted.

Standard production architecture for visualization: Frontend (Web Tier): Runs Nginx. Receives external traffic. Needs to talk to the Backend. Backend (Application Tier): Runs application logic (e.g., Python). Receives traffic from the Frontend. Needs to talk to the Database. Database (Data Tier): Runs MySQL. Receives traffic from the Backend. Should NOT be accessible by the Frontend directly.

NetworkPolicies are declarative. While Kubernetes stores the policy object, the CNI (Container Network Interface) plugin is responsible for the actual enforcement (blocking/allowing packets). CNIs that support Policies: Calico, Cilium, Antrea, AWS VPC CNI, Azure CNI. CNIs that DO NOT support Policies: Flannel, basic Kindnet. Check Command: kubectl get daemonset -n kube-system # Look for calico-node or cilium-agent

Ingress: Incoming traffic to a pod (e.g., traffic entering the Backend pod from the Frontend). Egress: Outgoing traffic from a pod (e.g., traffic leaving the Backend pod to reach the Database). Statefulness: Kubernetes NetworkPolicies are stateful. If you allow Ingress from Pod A to Pod B, the return (response) traffic from B back to A is automatically allowed. You do not need a separate Egress rule for the response.

NetworkPolicies use three methods to identify allowed traffic: podSelector: Identifies pods in the same namespace based on labels. podSelector: matchLabels: role: backend namespaceSelector: Identifies pods in different namespaces based on namespace labels. namespaceSelector: matchLabels: app: app1 ipBlock: Uses CIDR ranges for external sources/destinations outside the cluster. ipBlock: cidr: 10.0.0.0/24 except: - 10.0.0.5/32

Default KIND networking doesn't support policies. Disable Kindnet and install Calico. # kind-cluster.yaml kind: Cluster apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4 networking: disableDefaultCNI: true Install Calico: kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/projectcalico/calico/v3.30.2/manifests/calico.yaml
Create pods in the app1-ns namespace with clear labels: Frontend: role: frontend, app: app1 Backend: role: backend, app: app1 Database: role: db, app: app1

1. Database Policy (db-netpol.yaml)​ Goal: Allow only Backend pods to reach the Database on Port 3306. apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: NetworkPolicy metadata: name: db-policy namespace: app1-ns spec: podSelector: matchLabels: role: db # Target the DB pods policyTypes: - Ingress ingress: - from: - podSelector: matchLabels: role: backend # Only allow traffic from backend ports: - protocol: TCP port: 3306 2. Backend Policy (backend-netpol.yaml)​ Goal: Allow Ingress from Frontend and Egress to DB and DNS. apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: NetworkPolicy metadata: name: backend-policy namespace: app1-ns spec: podSelector: matchLabels: role: backend policyTypes: - Ingress - Egress ingress: - from: - podSelector: matchLabels: role: frontend ports: - protocol: TCP port: 5678 egress: - to: - podSelector: matchLabels: role: db ports: - protocol: TCP port: 3306 - to: # Allow DNS resolution - namespaceSelector: matchLabels: kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system podSelector: matchLabels: k8s-app: kube-dns ports: - protocol: UDP port: 53 - protocol: TCP port: 53

When a pod tries to reach db-svc, it first performs a DNS lookup via CoreDNS (running in kube-system). If your policy includes policyTypes: [Egress] but doesn't explicitly allow port 53 traffic to CoreDNS, the pod will fail to resolve the service name to an IP, breaking all service-to-service communication.

Traffic is allowed ONLY if it matches the Namespace AND the Pod Label. This is the Best Practice for DNS. - to: - namespaceSelector: matchLabels: kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system podSelector: matchLabels: k8s-app: kube-dns Meaning: Only talk to CoreDNS inside the kube-system namespace.

documents.t: Traffic is allowed if it matches the Namespace OR matches the Pod Label. Too Permissive. - to: - namespaceSelector: matchLabels: kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system - podSelector: matchLabels: k8s-app: kube-dns Risks: A pod outside kube-system can label itself k8s-app=kube-dns and receive traffic. Any pod inside kube-system can receive traffic even if it isn't CoreDNS.

Frontend DB 3306 Deny Not allowed in DB Ingress. DB Backend 5678 Deny DB has no Egress allowed; Backend Ingress restricted. Backend External IP 80 Deny Backend Egress only allows DB and DNS.

Implicit Deny: Once a policy targets a pod, all traffic not explicitly allowed is blocked. Namespace Scope: NetworkPolicies only apply to the namespace they are created in (unless using namespaceSelector). Stateful Nature: Don't write return rules; focus on the initiation of the connection. DNS Egress: Always include Port 53 rules if using an Egress policy. Selector Logic: A single list item with multiple selectors is an AND. Separate list items (starting with -) are an OR.

Kubernetes is designed with a modular and extensible architecture, which provides flexibility, scalability, and vendor neutrality. Core Components: Handle essential orchestration tasks. Extensions: Plugins, add-ons, and third-party tools enhance functionality without bloating the core.

API Server: The central hub; validates and serves REST API requests. Scheduler: Assigns Pods to Nodes based on resource availability and constraints. Controller Manager: Runs various control loops (e.g., ensuring desired replica count, managing endpoints). etcd: Distributed key-value store; persists the cluster state and configuration. Cloud Controller Manager (CCM): Manages cloud-specific resources (Load Balancers, persistent storage, node lifecycle) when running on a cloud provider.

kubelet: The primary agent on every node; ensures containers run as expected according to the PodSpec. kube-proxy: Manages network rules on the node for Pod/Service communication via proxy modes (iptables/IPVS).
Kubernetes achieves its flexibility through standardized interfaces that allow external components to integrate seamlessly.

These plugins use standardized interfaces to abstract away implementation details. CNI (Container Network Interface): Manages Pod networking (assigning IPs, inter-pod communication, network policies). CSI (Container Storage Interface): Manages external storage (provisioning, resizing, snapshots). CRI (Container Runtime Interface): Interfaces with actual container runtimes (like containerd, CRI-O).
documents.s: a) Plugins – Standardized APIs for External Integration

documents.t: Category Examples Runtimes (CRI) containerd, CRI-O, Kata Containers, gVisor Networking (CNI) Flannel, Calico, Cilium, Weave Net Storage (CSI) AWS EBS, Ceph, OpenEBS

These are general Kubernetes resources or controllers that enhance cluster functionality. Ingress Controllers: Manage external HTTP/S routing to internal Services. Monitoring: Tools for collecting and visualizing metrics (e.g., Prometheus, Grafana). Service Mesh: Provides advanced traffic management, security, and observability (e.g., Istio, Linkerd).

Tools that interact with Kubernetes to manage deployments or operations. Helm: Package manager for defining, installing, and upgrading even the most complex Kubernetes applications. Prometheus: A leading system for monitoring and alerting. Istio: A popular implementation of a Service Mesh.

Interface Primary Responsibilities CRI (Runtime) Pull images, start/stop/delete containers. Manage container-level resources, logging, and monitoring hooks. CNI (Networking) Assign Pod IPs, facilitate inter-node communication. Enforce network policies, integrate with DNS resolution, and support network observability. CSI (Storage) Provision/mount volumes, handle volume resizing, manage volume snapshots. Ensure data persistence across Pod restarts and manage access controls.

The reliance on interfaces (CRI, CNI, CSI) is central to Kubernetes' success: Interoperability: Works with multiple container runtimes, diverse networking solutions, and various storage backends. Flexibility/Vendor Neutrality: Avoids vendor lock-in by allowing users to swap out implementations (e.g., use Calico today, switch to Cilium tomorrow). Encourages Innovation: Independent plugin development allows the ecosystem to evolve rapidly (e.g., new CNI solutions). Scalability & Maintainability: The core is kept lean, and individual components can be upgraded or scaled modularly. Example: Cilium, a CNI plugin using eBPF, enhances network security and observability without requiring modifications to Kubernetes' core networking model. This level of extensibility allows Kubernetes to adapt seamlessly across different infrastructure environments.
Health probes are mechanisms managed by the kubelet to check the status of containers within a Pod.

Probe Type Checks For Action on Failure Runs During Use Cases Readiness If the container is ready to serve traffic. Marks Pod Unready (removes from Service Endpoints). Container is NOT restarted. Continuously throughout the Pod's lifecycle. DB Connection, Application initialization, Temporary Overload. Liveness If the container is alive and functioning properly. Restarts the failed container. Other containers in the Pod remain unaffected. Continuously throughout the Pod's lifecycle. Deadlock Detection, Unresponsive States, Memory Leaks (apps stuck in OOM errors). Startup If the container has enough time to initialize the application. Restarts if the probe fails. Only runs until it succeeds once. Legacy/Slow-Starting Apps, Resource-Intensive Apps, Large Data Loading Jobs. Readiness Probes: If any single container inside the Pod fails its readiness check, the entire Pod is marked as 'Not Ready' and removed from Service Endpoints, but the container is not restarted. Liveness Probes: If a Liveness probe fails, the particular container is restarted by the kubelet. Startup Probes: Readiness and Liveness probes only start running after the Startup Probe succeeds.

These properties are common across Readiness, Liveness, and Startup probes. Property Meaning Default Value Example initialDelaySeconds Wait time before the first probe starts after the container starts. 0 seconds initialDelaySeconds: 5 $\rightarrow$ starts after 5 sec periodSeconds Time interval between probe attempts. 10 seconds periodSeconds: 10 $\rightarrow$ probes every 10 sec timeoutSeconds Max wait time for probe response. 1 second timeoutSeconds: 2 $\rightarrow$ fail if no reply in 2 sec successThreshold No. of consecutive successes needed to mark probe as successful. 1 successThreshold: 3 $\rightarrow$ pass after 3 successes failureThreshold No. of consecutive failures before marking probe as failed. 3 failureThreshold: 5 $\rightarrow$ fail after 5 failures
(Supported by RP, LP & SP) There are three ways to execute a probe:

The kubelet sends an HTTP GET request to a specified endpoint. Success: Status codes 200–399. Failure: Any other status code (e.g., 404, 500). Example (Liveness Probe): livenessProbe: httpGet: path: /healthz port: 8080 httpHeaders: - name: Custom-Header value: Awesome initialDelaySeconds: 3 periodSeconds: 3 timeoutSeconds: 1 failureThreshold: 1

The kubelet checks if a TCP connection can be established to a specified port. Success: Connection is established. Failure: Connection cannot be established. Use Case: Useful for services like databases that listen on specific ports. Example (Startup Probe): startupProbe: tcpSocket: port: 9444 failureThreshold: 15 periodSeconds: 5 Probe waits until a TCP connection can be established on port 9444. Can be used for legacy/slow-starting applications.

The kubelet runs a specified command inside the container. Success: Command exits with code 0. Failure: Command exits with a non-zero code. Example (Readiness Probe): readinessProbe: exec: command: - cat - /tmp/ready initialDelaySeconds: 5 periodSeconds: 5 failureThreshold: 1 This runs cat /tmp/ready. If the file exists, the command exits 0 (Success); otherwise, it exits non-zero (Failure).

1. Readiness Probe with Command Execution​ This Pod creates a file /tmp/ready after 3 seconds, making it ready. apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: readiness-probe-demo spec: containers: - name: busybox-app image: busybox command: ["sh", "-c", "touch /tmp/ready; sleep 3600"] # Creates file then keeps running readinessProbe: exec: command: - cat - /tmp/ready initialDelaySeconds: 5 # Wait 5 seconds before the first probe periodSeconds: 5 # Probe runs every 5 seconds failureThreshold: 1 # Mark pod as NotReady after 1 failure To simulate failure: kubectl exec -it readiness-probe-demo -- rm /tmp/ready. 2. Liveness Probe with HTTP Get​ This example shows a Liveness probe that checks /healthz on port 8080 and sends a custom header. Crucially, the behavior of the endpoint changes over time: For the first 10 seconds, the endpoint returns 200 (Success). After 10 seconds, it returns 500 (Failure), which will cause the container to be restarted due to failureThreshold: 1. apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: liveness-probe-demo labels: test: liveness spec: containers: - name: liveness image: registry.k8s.io/e2e-test-images/agnhost:2.40 args: ["liveness"] livenessProbe: httpGet: path: /healthz port: 8080 httpHeaders: - name: Custom-Header value: Awesome initialDelaySeconds: 3 # Wait 3 seconds before starting probes periodSeconds: 3 # Run the probe every 3 seconds timeoutSeconds: 1 # Wait 1 second for a response before timing out failureThreshold: 1 # After 1 failure, restart the container 3. Startup Probe with TCP Socket​ This probe is designed for slow-starting applications that need a long time before they can even respond to a Liveness or Readiness check. apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: startup-probe-demo spec: containers: - name: tcp-app image: ubuntu:latest command: - sh - -c - | apt update && \ apt install -y netcat-openbsd && \ nc -l -p 9444 && \ sleep 3600 startupProbe: tcpSocket: port: 9444 failureThreshold: 15 # Allows up to 15 failed attempts (15 * 5s = 75 seconds total initial check time) periodSeconds: 5 # Probe runs every 5 seconds The probe waits until the TCP server (port 9444) is ready, allowing the slow startup commands to complete before Liveness/Readiness checks begin.

Scaling adjusts application resources based on load. Goal: Meet demand without over-provisioning. Elastic scaling: Scale up on high load, scale down on low load. Scaling Types:​ Horizontal Scaling: Changing the Number of replicas (Pods/VMs). Scaling Out: Adding more instances/pods. Scaling In: Removing instances/pods when load decreases. Vertical Scaling: Changing the CPU/Memory resources of the existing Pod or VM. Often requires the Pod/VM to restart for new resource requests to take effect. Scaling Approaches:​ Scaling Type For Worker Nodes For Pods (Automatic) For Pods (Manual) Horizontal Cluster Autoscaler, Karpenter HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler) Use kubectl scale deploy/my-deploy --replicas=2 Vertical (Disruptive, generally avoided) VPA (Vertical Pod Autoscaler) Changing the requests & limits in the manifest
Adjusts Pod replicas based on observed metrics. The HPA Controller runs a control loop checking metrics every 15 seconds. Works with Deployment, StatefulSet, ReplicaSet, and ReplicationController.
HPA needs CPU/memory requests defined on the Pods to calculate the utilization percentage. Without requests, HPA has no baseline for scaling.

cAdvisor collects usage on node. kubelet exposes metrics. Metrics Server aggregates metrics. HPA queries Metrics Server and makes scaling decisions. Custom Metrics Categories:​ Type Description API Used Internal Custom Metrics Metrics tied to Kubernetes objects (like pods or deployments). Custom Metrics API External Metrics Metrics not related to Kubernetes objects (external systems, APIs, etc.). External Metrics API Configuration: apiVersion: autoscaling/v2 kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler metadata: name: nginx-hpa spec: scaleTargetRef: apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment name: hpa-deploy minReplicas: 1 maxReplicas: 10 metrics: - type: Resource resource: name: cpu target: type: Utilization averageUtilization: 50

Create Deployment (nginx-deploy) with CPU requests/limits: # ... snippet from deployment manifest resources: requests: cpu: "100m" limits: cpu: "200m" Expose with ClusterIP Service (nginx-svc). Create HPA: Set target utilization to 50% of requests, with min 1 pod, max 5 pods. kubectl autoscale deployment nginx-deploy --cpu-percent=50 --min=1 --max=5 Behavior: If average CPU usage $> 50%$, HPA scales out (adds pods, up to max 5). If average CPU usage $< 50%$, HPA scales in (removes pods, but maintains minimum 1). Load Generation Example: kubectl run -it --rm load-generator --image=busybox /bin/sh -- while true; do wget -q -O- http://nginx-svc; done Note: Kubernetes defaults to targeting 80% CPU usage if --cpu-percent is not specified.

Function: Automatically adjusts CPU/memory requests (and optionally limits) for Pods based on historical usage. Behavior: Restarts Pods to apply changes (unless in a specific mode). Useful when manual tuning of resource requests is difficult.

Mode Behavior Off Only provides recommendations. Safe for production. Initial Sets values at pod creation only. No updates afterward. Auto Continuously updates resources and restarts pods as needed. Note: In Auto mode with 1 replica, VPA may be configured to avoid restarts to prevent downtime.

Recommender: Analyzes and suggests optimal values. Updater: Evicts pods when needed (respects Pod Disruption Budgets). Admission Controller: Modifies Pod specs upon creation if a VPA applies to the namespace.

Create NGINX Deployment with 2 replicas. Apply VPA object configured for updateMode: Auto. apiVersion: autoscaling.k8s.io/v1 kind: VerticalPodAutoscaler metadata: name: nginx-vpa spec: targetRef: apiVersion: "apps/v1" kind: Deployment name: nginx-deploy updatePolicy: updateMode: "Auto" # VPA automatically updates resources and restarts pods as needed. Observe recommendations: kubectl describe vpa

Feature HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler) VPA (Vertical Pod Autoscaler) Type of scaling Number of replicas (Pods) CPU/memory of a pod Resources monitored CPU, memory, custom metrics CPU, memory Resource adjusted Number of pods CPU/memory requests/limits Pod restart required No Yes (for changes to take effect) Components required Metrics Server VPA Recommender, Updater, Admission Controller Ideal use case Variable workloads, web APIs, microservices Batch jobs, ML workloads, stable workloads with hard-to-tune requests Compatibility Combination possible with Caution Combination possible with Caution

When a Pod is deleted (via kubectl delete pod or scaling down), Kubernetes initiates a graceful termination sequence rather than an abrupt shutdown. SIGTERM Signal: Kubernetes first sends a SIGTERM signal to the main process of each container inside the Pod, instructing the application to shut down gracefully. Termination Grace Period: By default, Kubernetes waits for 30 seconds (terminationGracePeriodSeconds defined in the Pod spec) for the container to exit cleanly after receiving SIGTERM. SIGKILL Signal: If the container does not exit within the grace period, Kubernetes sends a SIGKILL signal to force an immediate, abrupt shutdown.

You can force an immediate deletion, which sends SIGKILL right away without waiting for the grace period: kubectl delete po <pod-name> --force=true --grace-period=0 This immediately removes the Pod from the API server and instructs the container runtime to kill the container without giving the application time to shut down gracefully.

The restartPolicy is defined at the Pod-level and applies to all containers within that Pod. Kubernetes watches the container's exit code: 0 indicates success, and a non-zero status code indicates failure. Restart Policy Behavior Use Case Always The container will be restarted regardless of its exit code (0 or non-zero). Continuous availability needs (e.g., web servers, application pods). OnFailure The container will be restarted only if it exits with a non-zero status code. Data processing, batch jobs, or cronjobs that should only be retried upon failure. Never The container will not be restarted regardless of its exit code. One-time diagnosis pods or tasks that should terminate permanently upon completion or failure.

This is defined at the Container-level (spec.containers.imagePullPolicy). Policy Behavior Use Case Always Kubernetes will always pull the image from the registry, even if a matching image is already present on the node. Development/Testing: Ensures you are working with the absolute latest image changes from the registry. IfNotPresent Kubernetes will pull the image only if the image is not present on the Node. If it's already cached locally, it will use the cached version. Production: Ideal for faster startup times when using specific tags (like v1.2.3). Never Kubernetes will never pull the image from the registry, assuming the image is preloaded on the Node. Air-gapped environments where nodes are preloaded with container images.

For containers using the :latest tag, the default imagePullPolicy is Always, regardless of what is explicitly written in the spec. This is a safety measure to ensure that :latest always pulls the absolute latest version available.

documents.t: Pods move through distinct phases throughout their existence, tracked internally by Kubernetes. Phase Description Pending The Pod has been accepted by the cluster, but one or more containers have not been created yet (e.g., waiting for resources, pulling images). ContainerCreating (Internal Tracking) The Kubelet is in the process of pulling images and creating the containers. Running The Pod has been bound to a Node, and all containers have been created. At least one container is running or is in the process of starting or restarting. Succeeded (Internal Tracking) All containers in the Pod terminated successfully (only for Pods with restartPolicy: Never or if they are Jobs). Completed (User-friendly representation) The Pod has finished its work successfully (corresponds to the internal Succeeded phase). Failed All containers in the Pod have terminated, and at least one container terminated in failure (non-zero exit code). Unknown The state of the Pod could not be obtained (usually due to node failure).

A Pod is a logical layer to group one or more containers sharing a common network namespace and shared storage. A multi-container Pod typically has one main/primary container and one or more helper containers.

Resource Shared in Pod? Explanation Network Namespace $\checkmark$ Yes All containers share the same network namespace. Communicate over localhost or the Pod's IP. Example: Helper container accesses the main container on localhost:<port>. Volumes/Storage $\checkmark$ Yes Volumes are defined at the Pod level. Any container mounting the volume can access the data. Example: Sidecar reads logs written by the main container. PID Namespace $\times$ No Each container has its own process namespace (isolated from others, unless hostPID: true is configured). Filesystem (Root FS) $\times$ No Every container has its own root filesystem. Shared access is only possible via explicitly mounted volumes. Environment Variables $\times$ No Environment variables are scoped to each container. Can be shared across containers using ConfigMaps or Secrets if needed. Note: Setting shareProcessNamespace: true allows containers in the same Pod to see each other's processes (e.g., for sending signals using kill). Example Pod with shareProcessNamespace: true: apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: nginx spec: shareProcessNamespace: true containers: - name: nginx image: nginx - name: shell image: busybox:1.28 command: ["sleep", "3600"] securityContext: capabilities: add: - SYS_PTRACE # Example capability for process tracing stdin: true tty: true

Lifecycle: Startup containers designed to run before the main application container(s). They always run to completion (success or failure). Order of Execution: If multiple Init Containers exist, they run sequentially, one after the other. Dependency: The main/primary container will not start unless all Init Containers complete successfully (exit code 0). Use Cases (Preconditions Check): Database readiness (verify DB connection or schema migration). External API health checks. File or directory initialization. Fetching secrets/configurations from external systems. Cleaning up temporary files from a previous run. Note: You cannot exec into Init Containers as they stop and are removed upon completion. Example Init Containers (Checking External API and Internal Service DNS): This Pod will only start the main-app (nginx) container once the external API is available AND the internal service DNS can be resolved. apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: init-demo-2 labels: app: main-app spec: initContainers: - name: check-api image: curlimages/curl:latest command: - sh - -c - | echo 'Checking external API availability...' sleep 25 until curl -s https://kubernetes.io > /dev/null; do echo 'Waiting for external API...' sleep 5 done echo 'External API is accessible, proceeding to next init container!' - name: check-svc image: curlimages/curl:latest command: - sh - -c - | echo 'Checking main-app Service availability...' until nslookup main-app-svc.default.svc.cluster.local; do echo 'Waiting for Service DNS resolution...' sleep 5 done echo 'Service is reachable, proceeding to main-app container!' containers: - name: main-app image: nginx:latest

Purpose: Extend or complement the functionality of the main/primary container. They run alongside it and operate independently. Use Cases: Logging: Collecting logs and sending them to a central system (like fluentd or fluentbit). Monitoring: Exporting metrics for tools like Prometheus. Proxying: Handling incoming traffic (often managed by the primary container). Data Synchronisation. Example Sidecar (Health Logger): The sidecar monitors the main app's health on port 80 and reports its status independently. apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: sidecar-logging-demo spec: containers: # Main application container - name: main-app image: nginx:latest ports: - containerPort: 80 # Sidecar container - name: health-logger image: curlimages/curl:latest command: - sh - -c - | while true; do curl -s http://localhost:80 > /dev/null && echo 'Main app is healthy' || echo 'Main app is unhealthy' sleep 5 done If the main app fails (e.g., you kill 1 from inside the main-app container), the sidecar logs 'Main app is unhealthy'.

Involves: Containers that act as proxies between the Pod and external systems. Focus: Sidecars focus on internal cluster communication; Ambassadors focus on handling external communication. Use Cases: API Gateways: Proxying external client requests to internal services (routing based on paths or headers). Connection Management: Optimizing and pooling connections to external resources (like databases or APIs). Security: Terminating TLS and handling OAuth token validation before forwarding requests. Aspect Sidecar Pattern Ambassador Pattern Scope Internal cluster communication External system communication Primary Use Case Enhance the functionality of the main container Mediate communication between pod and external systems Example Envoy managing traffic between microservices Ambassador proxying requests to external APIs

Involves: Containers that transform or normalize data flowing between the main container and the external system. Use Cases: Metric Transformation: Convert custom application metrics into standard formats like Prometheus. Log Normalisation: Process and format logs for external logging systems.

Aspect Init Containers Sidecar / Ambassador / Adapter Containers Lifecycle Run to completion before main container starts. Run alongside the main container, continue as long as the Pod runs. Order of Execution Always run before the main container, in sequence if multiple. Start in parallel with the main container. Dependency on Success Main container won't start unless all inits complete successfully. Main container can run independently (but may rely on helper functionality). Restart Behavior Re-run only if they fail before completion. Restart policies apply same as the main container (Always, OnFailure, etc.). Purpose Setup, preparation, environment bootstrapping, precondition checks. Enhance, complement, or adapt runtime behavior of the main container. Resource Consumption Consume resources temporarily, freed once completed. Consume resources throughout the pod's lifetime. Common Use-Cases Database migrations, Configuration fetch, Waiting for dependencies. Log collection, Proxying (Service Mesh), External communication handling. Visibility to Main Container Prepare shared volumes or environment; not visible as active containers. Main container and helpers can interact live via shared network & volumes. Fail Impact Pod won't proceed if an init container fails. If they fail, the Pod continues, but functionality (e.g., logging, proxying) may degrade.

documents.t: Purpose: Define CPU/Memory guarantees (Requests) and ceilings (Limits) for Pods.

1. CPU Units​ 1 CPU = 1 vCPU/core (AWS/Azure/GCP) = 1 Hyperthread (Intel). Millicores (m): Used to express fractions of a CPU. 1000m = 1 CPU. 500m = 0.5 CPU. 2. Memory Units​ Memory is measured in powers of 1024 (binary prefixes, Ki, Mi, Gi). Unit Equivalent Example Gi 1 Gibibyte = 1024 Mi 2Gi = 2048Mi Mi 1 Mebibyte = 1024 Ki 512Mi Ki 1 Kibibyte = 1024 bytes 256Ki G 1 Gigabyte = 1000 MB (Avoid: Use Gi) M 1 Megabyte = 1000 KB (Avoid: Use Mi)

Requests: Minimum resources guaranteed to a container inside a Pod. This is used by the Scheduler for making the placement decision. Limits: Maximum resources a container inside a Pod can use. This is enforced by the kubelet on the node.
Resource Exceeding Request Exceeding Limit CPU Throttled (not killed) Throttled to the limit Memory May be evicted if the node is under pressure (low priority) OOMKilled (container restarts)

If a Pod specifies limits but no requests, Kubernetes defaults the Requests to equal the Limits. apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: complex-pod spec: containers: - name: main image: nginx resources: limits: cpu: "200m" memory: "512Mi" - name: sidecar image: alpine command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 3600"] resources: requests: cpu: "100m" memory: "128Mi" Total Requests: main (0 CPU) + sidecar (100m CPU) = 100m CPU request (Note: The example text says total limits are 300m, but based on the manifest above, the actual total request is 100m, and total limit is 300m). For predictable scheduling, Requests should ideally match Limits.

Metrics are collected for monitoring usage, not for scheduling decisions (that's what Requests are for). cAdvisor: A built-in component of the kubelet binary that collects raw resource usage statistics (CPU, memory, filesystem, network) for containers on its node. Metrics Server: A cluster-wide aggregator that collects data from all kubelets and exposes it via the standard metrics.k8s.io API, which HPA and kubectl top use. It stores only short-term metrics. kubectl top nodes Output Columns: Column Meaning NAME The node name or IP address. CPU(cores) Current CPU usage in millicores (m). (1000m = 1 CPU core). CPU(%) Percentage of total allocatable CPU currently in use. MEMORY(bytes) Current memory usage in MiB (Mebibytes). MEMORY(%) Percentage of total allocatable memory currently in use. Commands for Resource Checks: Check Pod resource usage: kubectl top pod <pod-name> Describe node resources and check allocatable amount: kubectl describe nodes | grep -A 10 "Allocated resources"

Purpose: Enforce default/min/max resources for Pods/Containers within a specific namespace. They are namespace-scoped objects. What It Does: Sets default requests/limits if they are omitted in a Pod spec. Rejects Pods that try to set requests or limits outside the namespace's defined min/max rules. Prevents resource starvation or creation of excessively large Pods in shared clusters. Example LimitRange YAML: apiVersion: v1 kind: LimitRange metadata: name: my-limits spec: limits: - type: Container min: { cpu: "100m", memory: "100Mi" } # Minimum allowed max: { cpu: "2", memory: "2Gi" } # Maximum allowed default: { cpu: "500m", memory: "512Mi" } # Default limits if omitted Memory Limit Enforcement Detail: A container exceeding its memory Limit gets terminated by the Linux Kernel's cgroup OOM Killer, independently of the node's overall memory status. Commands: Apply LimitRange: kubectl apply -f limitrange.yaml Verify setup: kubectl describe limitrange my-limitrange

Purpose: Restrict total resource consumption per namespace. They will specify hard limits. Example ResourceQuota YAML: apiVersion: v1 kind: ResourceQuota metadata: name: my-quota spec: hard: requests.cpu: "10" # Max 10 CPU requests in namespace requests.memory: 20Gi limits.cpu: "20" limits.memory: 40Gi pods: "50" # Max 50 Pods in namespace A quota of "0" pods effectively locks the namespace from running any workloads. Key Differences: LimitRange vs. ResourceQuota Feature LimitRange ResourceQuota Scope Per-container/Pod in a namespace Aggregated per namespace Enforces Min/max/default resources Total resource caps Use Case Prevent tiny/huge Pods; Set defaults Prevent namespace resource abuse Notes on Resource Management: Always set requests $\approx$ limits for predictable scheduling (avoid the "noisy neighbor" problem). Monitor OOMKills: Adjust memory limits if frequent restarts occur. Use LimitRange to enforce defaults (e.g., for dev vs. prod namespaces). Combine with HorizontalPodAutoscaler (HPA) for dynamic scaling. Pro Tip: Use kubectl describe nodes to debug scheduling failures (e.g., "Insufficient cpu/memory").
The Kubernetes Scheduler automatically assigns Pods to Nodes based on the following criteria: Resource availability (CPU, memory). Taints & Tolerations. Affinity/Anti-affinity rules.
You can force a Pod to run on a specific node using manual scheduling: How? By setting the nodeName field in the Pod specification: spec: nodeName: my-node-name

Check Nodes: kubectl get nodes Apply Manifest: kubectl apply -f <file>.yaml Verify Pod Location: kubectl get pods -o wide Note: If the node specified by nodeName is invalid or unavailable, the Pod will remain in Pending status. It might eventually be deleted over time via Kubernetes garbage collection policies. You can manually schedule Pods on control-plane nodes (despite their taints) by explicitly setting .spec.nodeName. Control Plane Nodes Run: kubelet (executes static/manual pods). kube-proxy (handles networking).

Definition: Pods that are managed directly by the kubelet agent on a node and not by the Kube API Server. Use Case: Primarily used for bootstrapping and running control plane components (e.g., kube-apiserver, etcd). Resilience: They run even if the API server is down. Defined At: Manifest files are placed in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ on the node. Managed By: kubelet (the API Server is unaware of them initially). Immutability: Cannot be modified or deleted via kubectl commands (like kubectl edit or kubectl delete).

Creation: kubelet creates a Mirror Pod object in the API Server to represent the static pod, allowing it to be viewed via kubectl. Status: Mirror Pods are Read-only; you cannot modify or delete them via kubectl. Naming: Mirror Pods are typically named as: <pod-name>-<node-hostname> (for example: dashboard-proxy-node01).

To create a static pod named nginx-static-pod on the node where you execute the command: cat <<EOF > /etc/kubernetes/manifests/static-pod.yaml apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: nginx-static-pod spec: containers: - name: nginx-container image: nginx ports: - containerPort: 80 EOF Verify: After creating the file, kubelet will pick it up and create the corresponding Mirror Pod: kubectl get pods -A To Permanently Delete: You must remove the manifest file itself. Deleting the Mirror Pod via kubectl delete will only remove the mirror, and kubelet will immediately recreate it. rm -f /etc/kubernetes/manifests/static-pod.yaml
In Production (or bare-metal/VM setups): To manage static pods, you typically need to Access the node via SSH and directly Edit/Remove the static pod manifests located at /etc/kubernetes/manifests/.

Managing the cluster requires the ability to safely remove nodes for updates or repairs. kubectl cordon <node>: Marks the node as unschedulable. It does not affect existing pods. kubectl uncordon <node>: Reverses a cordon, allowing the scheduler to place new pods on the node again. kubectl drain <node>: The professional way to empty a node. It cordons the node and evicts all running pods. Safeguard Flags: --ignore-daemonsets: Since DaemonSets run on every node, they can't be "moved." This flag is required to bypass them. --delete-emptydir-data: Required if pods use local emptyDir volumes (the data will be deleted). --force: If there are pods not managed by a Controller (naked pods), you must use this to delete them.
