documents.t: Concept: A Node "Taint" tells pods: "Stay away unless you have a specific pass (Toleration)."

NoSchedule: (Hard) New pods without toleration will never be scheduled here. PreferNoSchedule: (Soft) The system tries to avoid placement but will land here if no other nodes are available. NoExecute: (Eviction) New pods are blocked, AND existing pods without the toleration are immediately kicked off the node.
If a node is tainted with hardware=nvidia-tesla:NoSchedule: spec: tolerations: - key: "hardware" operator: "Equal" value: "nvidia-tesla" effect: "NoSchedule"
documents.s: YAML Example: Tolerating a GPU Taint

documents.t: Simple key-value matching. If the label isn't there, the pod stays Pending. spec: nodeSelector: disktype: ssd

Node Affinity provides complex logic and levels of "strictness." Hard Rule: requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution​ The pod must meet these criteria, or it will remain in a Pending state. spec: affinity: nodeAffinity: requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution: nodeSelectorTerms: - matchExpressions: - key: topology.kubernetes.io/zone operator: In values: ["us-east-1a", "us-east-1b"] Soft Rule: preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution​ A "Best Effort" approach. You provide a Weight (1-100). The scheduler adds up weights for nodes that match and picks the highest score. If no nodes match, the pod is scheduled anyway. spec: affinity: nodeAffinity: preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution: - weight: 80 preference: matchExpressions: - key: disktype operator: In values: ["ssd"] Node Anti-Affinity​ To ensure a pod never lands on specific nodes, use NotIn or DoesNotExist inside a Hard Rule. requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution: nodeSelectorTerms: - matchExpressions: - key: kubernetes.io/hostname operator: NotIn values: ["master-node"]

This schedules pods based on the labels of other Pods already running on the node. Pod Affinity: "Run me where app: frontend is running" (Co-location for performance). Pod Anti-Affinity: "Do NOT run me where app: database is running" (Separation for HA).
This defines the scope of "closeness." kubernetes.io/hostname: The same physical node. topology.kubernetes.io/zone: The same Availability Zone.

Ensure two instances of the same app never run on the same node. spec: affinity: podAntiAffinity: requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution: - labelSelector: matchLabels: app: web-server topologyKey: "kubernetes.io/hostname"
While Anti-Affinity is "all or nothing," Topology Spread Constraints allow you to distribute pods evenly across zones or nodes to prevent bottlenecks.

maxSkew: The maximum difference in pod count between any two domains. maxSkew: 1 is ideal for balance. whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule: Hard rule (Pod stays Pending if balance can't be met). ScheduleAnyway: Soft rule (Still tries to balance but will schedule if it can't).
spec: topologySpreadConstraints: - maxSkew: 1 topologyKey: "topology.kubernetes.io/zone" whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule labelSelector: matchLabels: app: api-service

Feature Hard Rule (required...) Soft Rule (preferred...) Strictness Mandatory Requirement. Preference/Wishlist. Failure Result Pod remains Pending. Pod schedules on any available node. Use Case Compliance, Hardware requirements (GPU), Safety. Cost optimization, "Nice-to-have" performance boosts. Scheduling Overhead Low (Quickly filters nodes). Higher (Must calculate and compare weights).

Feature Logic Direction Target Taints Repulsion Node to Pod Repels non-tolerant pods. Tolerations Immunity Pod to Node Allows pods to stay on tainted nodes. Node Affinity Attraction Pod to Node Forces/Prefers pods to specific nodes. Pod Affinity Co-location Pod to Pod Puts pods together (App + Cache). Pod Anti-Affinity Separation Pod to Pod Keeps pods apart (HA Replicas). Topology Spread Balancing Pod to Domain Spreads pods evenly (Zone/Rack/Node).

All Affinity and Spread rules have the suffix IgnoredDuringExecution. This means if a pod is already running and the labels on the node or other pods change, Kubernetes will NOT evict the pod. Only Taints with NoExecute will cause active eviction.

In production environments, container images are stored in private registries to protect intellectual property and ensure security. Kubernetes requires explicit authentication to pull these images. This is handled via imagePullSecrets and can be managed at either the Pod level or the ServiceAccount level.
documents.s: Image Pull Secrets - Pulling Private Images

documents.t: Image Registry: A centralized service for storing and distributing container images. Public: docker.io, ghcr.io Cloud-Native: Amazon ECR, Azure ACR, Google GCR/Artifact Registry. Self-Hosted: JFrog Artifactory, Sonatype Nexus, GitLab Container Registry. Repository: A named collection of related container images that typically represent different versions of the same application (e.g., ubuntu:20.04, ubuntu:22.04). Image: At its core, an image is just a repository + a specific tag/version.

Component Description Example Registry The centralized service storing images. docker.io, ghcr.io, *.ecr.aws Namespace The owner/organization on the registry. cloudwithvarjosh Repository Logical grouping of related images. my-python-app Tag Specific version or variant. v1.0.0, stable, latest Full Image Identifier Syntax: <registry>/<namespace>/<repository>:<tag>

Default Registry: Defaults to docker.io (Docker Hub). Default Namespace: Defaults to library/ (for official Docker Hub images). Default Tag: Defaults to latest. Note: Using latest is not recommended for production as it makes rollbacks and version tracking difficult.

When Kubernetes attempts to pull an image from a private registry without valid credentials, the Pod will fail with an ImagePullBackOff or ErrImagePull status. Reason: The Container Runtime Interface (CRI) receives a 401 Unauthorized or Insufficient Scope error from the registry. Debugging: Use kubectl describe pod <pod-name> to view events confirming the authentication failure.

Kubernetes does not pull images directly; it delegates the task to the Container Runtime (CRI) like containerd or CRI-O. The Kubelet identifies the image and any associated imagePullSecrets. The Kubelet fetches the secret credentials from the API server. The Kubelet passes these credentials to the CRI. The CRI authenticates with the registry and downloads the image layers.

Method Scope Configuration Pod-level Single Pod Defined in spec.imagePullSecrets in the Pod manifest. Default ServiceAccount Namespace-wide Patch the default SA to include the secret. All Pods in that NS inherit it. Custom ServiceAccount Workload-specific Create a new SA, attach the secret, and use spec.serviceAccountName.
from flask import Flask app = Flask(__name__) @app.route("/") def home(): return "Hello, Private Registry!" if __name__ == "__main__": app.run(host="0.0.0.0", port=5000)
FROM python:3.9-slim WORKDIR /app ADD app.py app.py RUN pip install flask EXPOSE 5000 CMD ["python", "app.py"]
docker build -t <your-username>/app1:1.0.0 . docker login docker push <your-username>/app1:1.0.0 Note: Ensure the repository visibility is set to Private in your Docker Hub settings.

kubectl create secret docker-registry dockerhub-secret \ --docker-server=https://index.docker.io/v1/ \ --docker-username=<your-username> \ --docker-password=<your-password> \ --docker-email=<your-email>

documents.t: apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: private-pod spec: containers: - name: app-container image: docker.io/<your-username>/app1:1.0.0 imagePullSecrets: - name: dockerhub-secret
This method avoids adding imagePullSecrets to every single Pod manifest.

kubectl create ns prod-ns kubectl create secret docker-registry dockerhub-secret \ --docker-server=https://index.docker.io/v1/ \ --docker-username=<your-username> \ --docker-password=<your-password> \ --docker-email=<your-email> \ -n prod-ns
kubectl patch serviceaccount default \ -n prod-ns \ -p '{"imagePullSecrets": [{"name": "dockerhub-secret"}]}'
apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: ns-pod namespace: prod-ns spec: containers: - name: app-container image: docker.io/<your-username>/app1:1.0.0
kubectl create serviceaccount custom-sa -n prod-ns kubectl patch serviceaccount custom-sa \ -n prod-ns \ -p '{"imagePullSecrets": [{"name": "dockerhub-secret"}]}'

documents.t: RBAC: Restrict get and list permissions on Secrets to only authorized users and ServiceAccounts. Namespace Isolation: Secrets are namespace-scoped. They do not share across namespaces unless explicitly recreated in the target namespace. Credential Rotation: Regularly update registry passwords or tokens and update the corresponding Kubernetes Secret objects. Cloud Native Identity: On AWS/GCP/Azure, prefer using IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA) or Workload Identity to avoid managing static password secrets. External Secrets: Use tools like HashiCorp Vault or AWS Secrets Manager with the External Secrets Operator to inject credentials into Kubernetes dynamically and securely.

Kubernetes makes running containers easy, but it does not secure them by default. Many container images run as the root user (UID 0), which creates significant risk. Pod Security ensures workloads run with the least privilege necessary, preventing misuse, accidental tampering, and potential container breakout.
documents.s: Pod Security - Security Context & Linux Capabilities

documents.t: Running containers as root is dangerous because: System Integrity: Root-level processes can modify system files. Escalation: A compromise can lead to full host privilege escalation. Access: Containers may gain unintended access to host resources. Compliance: Violates compliance and least-privilege security principles. Note: Some images run as non-root by default, but this should not be relied upon. Always enforce security explicitly through pod manifests and cluster policies.
Security Context defines privilege, identity, filesystem access, and escalation behavior for Pods and containers.

These settings apply to all containers inside the Pod. runAsUser: Sets the UID for all containers. (e.g., 1000). Recommendation: Use a non-zero UID to avoid running as root. runAsGroup: Sets the primary GID for container processes. Useful for managing file permissions. fsGroup: Assigns a supplemental GID to all processes. Kubernetes changes the ownership of mounted volumes to this GID and sets the setgid bit. Recommendation: Use this to allow non-root users access to shared mounted volumes. runAsNonRoot: Enforces that the container must run as a non-root user. If the image defaults to UID 0, the Pod will fail to start. Recommendation: Always set to true.

These settings apply to a specific container and override Pod-level settings. allowPrivilegeEscalation: Prevents processes from gaining more privileges than their parent process (e.g., via setuid binaries). Recommendation: Set to false. privileged: Grants the container full host access (all kernel capabilities, device access). Recommendation: Avoid unless absolutely necessary for low-level networking or storage operations. readOnlyRootFilesystem: Mounts the container's root filesystem as read-only. Recommendation: Set to true for stateless apps to prevent tampering. Use volumes for specific writable paths (logs/temp). capabilities: Used to add or drop specific Linux capabilities.

Field Pod Level Container Level Notes runAsUser ✅ ✅ Container overrides Pod runAsGroup ✅ ✅ Container overrides Pod runAsNonRoot ✅ ✅ Container overrides Pod fsGroup ✅ ❌ Pod-level only; affects volume ownership allowPrivilegeEscalation ❌ ✅ Container-level only privileged ❌ ✅ Container-level only readOnlyRootFilesystem ❌ ✅ Container-level only

apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: secure-pod spec: securityContext: # Pod-level runAsUser: 1000 runAsGroup: 3000 fsGroup: 2000 runAsNonRoot: true containers: - name: app image: busybox command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 3600"] securityContext: # Container-level allowPrivilegeEscalation: false readOnlyRootFilesystem: true

Identity: id command shows UID 1000, GID 3000, and supplemental group 2000. User Name: whoami fails because UID 1000 has no entry in /etc/passwd. Filesystem: Writing to / fails due to readOnlyRootFilesystem. Escalation: Sudo/Privilege escalation attempts are blocked.
To allow safe writes while keeping the root filesystem read-only (recommended for logs and caches):

spec: securityContext: runAsUser: 1000 fsGroup: 2000 containers: - name: app image: busybox securityContext: readOnlyRootFilesystem: true volumeMounts: - name: writable-vol mountPath: /writable volumes: - name: writable-vol emptyDir: {} Result: Writes to / fail. Writes to /writable succeed because fsGroup changed the group ownership of the volume to GID 2000 and the process belongs to that group.
Linux splits root privileges into granular units called Capabilities. By default, Docker/Kubernetes grant a small subset of these.

Capabilities are configured only under container.securityContext. Best Practice: Drop ALL capabilities and add back only the specific ones required. Running as UID 0 (root) without capabilities does not grant full root power.

NET_ADMIN: Network configuration (e.g., modifying interfaces). SYS_ADMIN: Broad system-level functions (dangerous). SYS_TIME: Modify system clock. CHOWN: Change file ownership. SETUID: Change process UID. DAC_OVERRIDE: Override file permission checks.

apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: cap-pod spec: containers: - name: app image: busybox command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 3600"] securityContext: allowPrivilegeEscalation: false capabilities: drop: - ALL # Drop everything first add: - NET_ADMIN - SYS_TIME
Success: NET_ADMIN operations (like bringing down a network interface) may work. Failure: chown operations will fail because CAP_CHOWN was dropped. This demonstrates precise privilege scoping.

Precedence: Container-level settings always win over Pod-level settings. Hardening: Use readOnlyRootFilesystem: true whenever possible to ensure immutability. Defaulting: If runAsNonRoot is true but the image doesn't specify a user, the Pod will crash. You must provide runAsUser. Audit: Use tools like kube-score or polaris to check if your manifests have these security fields defined. Standards: Kubernetes now uses Pod Security Standards (PSS) (Privileged, Baseline, Restricted) enforced via admission controllers to replace the deprecated PodSecurityPolicy (PSP).

Workload Classification: Not all applications have the same business value. Payment processors (critical) should take precedence over logging agents or development dashboards (non-critical). Resource Management: In a full cluster, if a critical pod cannot find space, the scheduler uses Preemption to reclaim resources from less important pods. Intelligent Scheduling: Priority guides the scheduler's queue; pods with higher priority are processed before those with lower priority.
documents.s: Why Pod Priority and Preemption Exist?

documents.t: A PriorityClass is a cluster-scoped object that maps a name to a numeric priority value. Numeric Value: Higher values represent higher priority. Value Range: For user-defined classes, the range is from -2,147,483,648 to 1,000,000,000. Global Default: Only one PriorityClass can be set as globalDefault: true. Pods without an explicit priorityClassName will inherit this value. If no global default exists, the priority of pods without a class is 0. System Classes: Kubernetes reserves values above 2 billion (e.g., 2,000,000,000) for system-critical components like etcd or kube-apiserver. Common ones include system-cluster-critical and system-node-critical.

Preemption occurs only when a high-priority pod is unschedulable due to insufficient resources. Eviction Process: The scheduler identifies lower-priority pods whose removal would free up enough resources. It triggers a graceful termination of those pods. Preemption Policy: By default, it is PreemptLowerPriority. However, you can set preemptionPolicy: Never. This allows a pod to move to the front of the scheduling queue (high priority) without being allowed to evict other running pods (non-preempting).

It is crucial to understand that Priority and QoS are two different mechanisms handled by different components: Feature Pod Priority QoS Class Controlled By Scheduler Kubelet Stage During pod placement (Scheduling) During runtime (Node pressure) Mechanism Preemption: Evicts lower-priority pods to make room for a new high-priority pod. Eviction: Evicts pods based on requests vs limits during resource pressure (e.g., OOM). Configuration PriorityClass resource and priorityClassName in pod spec. Based on requests and limits (Guaranteed, Burstable, BestEffort).

Cluster-Scoped: PriorityClasses are not restricted by namespaces. Reserved Values: Custom priorities must not exceed 1 billion. Values between 1 billion and 2 billion are reserved for internal Kubernetes use. Runtime Stability: Kubernetes does not proactively evict pods just because a high-priority class was created. Preemption is only triggered by the scheduling attempt of a new pod that cannot otherwise find space. Preemption respects PDBs: The scheduler tries to respect Pod Disruption Budgets (PDBs) when choosing victims, but it is not guaranteed.
Check existing classes used by the control plane. kubectl get pc kubectl describe pod -n kube-system <etcd-pod-name>

documents.t: Define the priority hierarchy for the cluster. apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1 kind: PriorityClass metadata: name: high-priority value: 1000 globalDefault: false description: "Critical production workloads." --- apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1 kind: PriorityClass metadata: name: low-priority value: 10 globalDefault: true description: "Default for non-critical workloads."

Deploy pods that consume a significant portion of the node's CPU to fill the cluster. apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: lp-nginx spec: replicas: 5 selector: matchLabels: app: nginx template: metadata: labels: app: nginx spec: containers: - name: nginx image: nginx:latest resources: requests: cpu: "1000m" # 1 vCPU per pod

Deploy high-priority pods with large resource requests to trigger eviction of the low-priority pods. # 03-high-priority-deployment.yaml apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: hp-nginx spec: replicas: 5 selector: matchLabels: app: nginx template: metadata: labels: app: nginx spec: priorityClassName: high-priority containers: - name: nginx image: nginx:latest resources: requests: cpu: "3000m" # 3 vCPUs per pod
documents.s: Step 4: Deploy High-Priority Pods and Observe Preemption

documents.t: kubectl get pods -w Observation: You will see lp-nginx pods entering the Terminating state as hp-nginx pods move from Pending to ContainerCreating.

Priority Range Category Usage > 2,000,000,000 System-Critical Reserved for kube-apiserver, etcd, kube-scheduler, etc. 1,000,001 - 2,000,000,000 Internal Reserved for Kubernetes internal components. -2,147,483,648 - 1,000,000,000 User-Defined Standard workloads (Critical to Batch).

Pod Preemption respects the terminationGracePeriodSeconds. If Pod A (Priority 1000) needs to preempt Pod B (Priority 500), but Pod B has a terminationGracePeriodSeconds of 300s, Pod A will be marked as "scheduled" (bound to the node) but cannot start its containers until Pod B's slot is physically empty after its grace period.

Purpose: Ensures that a specific Pod runs on every node (or a selected subset of nodes). It automatically manages Pod creation/deletion as nodes are added to or removed from the cluster. Self-Healing: If you delete a Pod created by a DaemonSet manually, the DaemonSet controller will immediately recreate it to maintain the desired state. Control Plane Scheduling: In managed cloud clusters (EKS, GKE, AKS), DaemonSets usually do not run on control plane nodes. On self-managed clusters, they can run on control plane nodes if the node has taints (e.g., node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule) and proper tolerations are configured in the Pod spec. Common Use Cases: Monitoring Agents: Prometheus Node Exporter, Datadog agent. Logging Agents: Fluentd, Fluent Bit, Filebeat. Networking Plugins: Calico, Flannel, Cilium. Storage Plugins: AWS EBS CSI, GCP PD CSI Drivers.

kube-proxy is deployed as a DaemonSet to ensure every node has networking functionality. Verification commands: kubectl get daemonsets.apps -n kube-system kube-proxy kubectl get pods -n kube-system -o wide | grep -i kube-proxy Tolerations in kube-proxy: Generally, it uses the following: tolerations: - operator: Exists Note: An operator of "Exists" with no key specified means the Pod tolerates any taint on the node—regardless of key, value, or effect. This ensures it can be scheduled everywhere.
kubectl create namespace logging-ns
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=logging-ns

apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: DaemonSet metadata: name: log-collector namespace: logging-ns labels: app: log-collector spec: selector: matchLabels: app: log-collector template: metadata: labels: app: log-collector spec: tolerations: - key: "node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane" operator: "Exists" effect: "NoSchedule" containers: - name: log-collector image: busybox command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "while true; do echo 'Collecting logs...'; sleep 30; done"] resources: requests: cpu: "50m" memory: "50Mi" limits: cpu: "100m" memory: "100Mi" volumeMounts: - name: varlog mountPath: /var/log volumes: - name: varlog hostPath: path: /var/log type: Directory Note: This uses hostPath to access the node's /var/log. In production, logs are usually shipped to external storage (S3, NFS) or platforms (ElasticSearch, Loki).

Purpose: A Job creates one or more Pods to run a specific task to completion. Once the task finishes successfully (Status = Completed), the Job is finished. Retries: If a Pod fails, the Job controller automatically retries the task based on the backoffLimit. Success: If a Pod succeeds, the Job does not restart it. Use Cases: Batch jobs, database migrations, generating reports.

apiVersion: batch/v1 kind: Job metadata: name: hello-job spec: ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 60 # Automatically deletes the job object 60s after completion completions: 2 # Total successful completions needed parallelism: 2 # Number of Pods that can run concurrently backoffLimit: 4 # Retries before marking the job as failed template: spec: containers: - name: hello image: busybox command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "echo Hello from the Job! && sleep 10"] restartPolicy: Never # Jobs usually use 'Never' or 'OnFailure'

Kubelet: Responsible for restarting containers within a Pod (if restartPolicy is Always/OnFailure). It does not recreate Pods. Job Controller: Detects failed Pods (at the API level) and decides whether to create a new Pod based on the backoffLimit. restartPolicy: Never: The Pod transitions to Failed phase on error, and the Job controller creates a new Pod.
documents.s: Key Logic: Kubelet vs. Job Controller

documents.t: Purpose: Allows you to schedule Jobs to run at specific times (like Linux crontab). Use Cases: Backups, nightly reports, cleanup tasks, scheduled notifications. Logic: It acts as a scheduler that creates a Job object at the specified time.

Position Field Allowed Values 1 Minute 0–59 2 Hour 0–23 3 Day of Month 1–31 4 Month 1–12 5 Day of Week 0–6 (0 = Sunday) * : Every value. /5 : Every 5 units (steps). 1,3,5 : Specific list. 1-5 : Range.
*/5 * * * * : Every 5 minutes. 0 * * * * : Every hour at minute 0. 0 2 * * * : Every day at 2 AM. 0 0 * * 0 : Every Sunday at midnight. Note: Kubernetes CronJobs use UTC time internally.

apiVersion: batch/v1 kind: CronJob metadata: name: hello-cronjob spec: schedule: "*/1 * * * *" # Every minute jobTemplate: spec: backoffLimit: 4 template: spec: containers: - name: hello image: busybox command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "echo Hello from CronJob!"] restartPolicy: Never

Aspect Deployment DaemonSet Job CronJob Purpose Long-running stateless apps with scaling. One Pod per node for infrastructure tasks. Run a task once to completion. Schedule Jobs at specific times. Common Use Cases Web servers, APIs. Monitoring, logging, networking. Migrations, backups, reports. Scheduled backups, nightly tasks. Examples Nginx, Node.js API. kube-proxy, Fluentd, Calico. DB migration, Backup script. Weekly reports, monthly invoices.

Purpose: Decouples configuration data (non-confidential) from container images. Usage: Stores key-value pairs or entire configuration files. Size Limit: Maximum size for a ConfigMap is 1MB. Consumption Methods: As environment variables: (Individual keys via valueFrom or all keys via envFrom). As command-line arguments: Used in the command or args section of a container. As configuration files via mounted volumes: Mounted as a directory or specific files. Note on Updates: Volumes: If a ConfigMap is mounted as a volume, Kubelet syncs it periodically (default ~1 min). The application must be able to "hot-reload" files to see changes without a restart. Env Vars: Environment variables are static. If the ConfigMap changes, you must restart the Pod (usually via a rollout) to see the new values.

1. Loading All Keys at Once (envFrom)​ Instead of mapping every key manually, use envFrom to inject all keys as environment variables automatically. spec: containers: - name: app-container image: nginx envFrom: - configMapRef: name: frontend-cm 2. Advanced Mounting with items:​ The items section allows you to project specific keys into specific file paths and even rename the files. volumes: - name: config-volume configMap: name: frontend-cm items: - key: index.html path: startup-page.html # The key 'index.html' is renamed to 'startup-page.html' on disk - key: APP path: app_name.txt 3. Immutable ConfigMaps (v1.19+)​ For clusters where configuration shouldn't change, you can mark a ConfigMap as immutable. This improves performance (Kubelet stops polling for changes) and prevents accidental edits. apiVersion: v1 kind: ConfigMap metadata: name: static-config immutable: true data: version: "1.0"

Purpose: Stores sensitive information (passwords, tokens, keys). Encoding: Data is Base64 encoded, not encrypted. Types of Secrets: Type Usage Opaque Default type for user-defined arbitrary key-value pairs. kubernetes.io/service-account-token Used for ServiceAccount credentials. kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson Used for imagePullSecrets to authenticate with private registries. kubernetes.io/basic-auth For username/password authentication. kubernetes.io/ssh-auth For SSH private keys. kubernetes.io/tls For storing TLS certificates and keys.

1. Data vs StringData​ data: Values must be manually base64 encoded. stringData: Allows you to write plain-text values. Kubernetes will base64 encode them automatically when you apply the manifest. (Note: stringData is write-only; it becomes data when you get the secret later). apiVersion: v1 kind: Secret metadata: name: db-secret type: Opaque stringData: password: "PlaintextPassword123" # Kubernetes encodes this for you 2. Using Image Pull Secrets​ To pull an image from a private Docker Registry: spec: imagePullSecrets: - name: my-registry-key containers: - name: private-app image: my-private-repo/app:v1 3. Mounting Secrets with Renaming (items:)​ volumes: - name: cert-volume secret: secretName: frontend-secret items: - key: DB_PASSWORD path: db_pass.txt # Mounts the password key into a file named db_pass.txt

Scope: Both are Namespace-scoped resources. Size: Both have a 1MB limit. Security: Secrets are stored in tmpfs (RAM) on the Node, so they aren't written to the Node's physical disk. Always enable Encryption at Rest in etcd for Secrets. SubPath Update Issue: If you use subPath to mount a single file from a ConfigMap/Secret, that file will not update automatically when the source changes (unlike a full directory mount). Immutability: Once set to immutable: true, you cannot change the data or stringData. You must delete and recreate the resource. Usage with envFrom: If a key in the ConfigMap/Secret is "invalid" as an env var name (e.g., starts with a digit), that specific key will be skipped, but the Pod will still start.
Docker images are built from a series of layers.

Layer-Creating Instructions: These instructions create a new layer in the image. Examples: FROM, RUN, COPY, ADD. Note: Having many of these increases the final image size. Multi-stage builds are recommended to separate build-time instructions (which create layers) from runtime instructions, producing smaller, optimized images. Non-Layer-Creating Instructions: These modify the behavior or metadata of the layer they are executed on, without creating a new layer themselves. Examples: CMD, ENTRYPOINT, WORKDIR, EXPOSE, ENV, LABEL, USER, VOLUME, STOPSIGNAL, ARG.

The layers created by FROM, RUN, ADD, etc., are Read-Only for all containers started from that image. When a container runs, any new files created or changes made are stored in a writable layer on the Docker Host. This is called delta data. Storage Usage Example: If the base image is 50MB, and Container 1 adds 4MB of delta data, the total storage used by Container 1 is 54 MB. Ephemeral Data: Since the delta data lives only in the writable layer, if the container is stopped or fails, this data is lost. A mechanism is needed to persist data beyond the container's lifecycle. Inspection: You can inspect the layers and storage history using: docker inspect history <image>
Docker manages storage using two primary driver types:

Handles: The container's internal ephemeral data (data tied to the container's lifecycle). Concept: Think of these as the Filesystems for Containers, managing the file organization within the container's root filesystem. Kubernetes Parallel: Kubernetes largely uses the same concepts for ephemeral container data. Examples (Common Drivers): OverlayFS (Default on modern Linux systems). ZFS (Advanced Storage). AUFS (Legacy Driver). Btrfs (For Large-Scale Environments). Checking Storage Driver: Run docker info to check the storage driver used by the Docker host.

Handles: External persistent data that exists independently of the container's lifecycle. Concept: Think of these as External Hard Drives for Containers. Kubernetes Parallel: Kubernetes manages this via Persistent Volumes (PVs), which are managed at the cluster-level rather than container-level. Examples: Local (Default Docker Volume Driver). NFS Cloud-specific drivers like AWS EBS or Azure Disks. Kubernetes Integration: Kubernetes uses CSI (Container Storage Interface) drivers to connect to cloud storage providers like AWS EBS, Azure Disks, or NFS, integrating them as PVs/PVCs. For temporary data, Kubernetes still relies on storage drivers similar to Docker (e.g., overlay2).

OS Docker Engine Requirement Storage Location Linux Runs natively, no virtualization layer required. Storage/volumes created directly on host filesystem: /var/lib/docker/volumes. macOS Docker Desktop uses a Linux VM via the Apple Virtualization Framework (previously HyperKit). Storage is inside the managed Linux VM. Windows Docker Desktop uses WSL 2 (Windows Subsystem for Linux) to run the Linux kernel. Storage is within the WSL 2 environment. Key takeaway: Docker Engine requires a native Linux kernel, which is why direct installation isn't possible on macOS or Windows without a virtualization/subsystem layer.

documents.t: Since container data in the writable layer is ephemeral (lost when the container is deleted), Docker volumes are used to persist data beyond the container lifecycle. Default Storage Location: /var/lib/docker/volumes on the Docker host.

Create a Docker volume: docker volume create my-vol Run a container attached to the volume: docker run -d --name my-cont-1 -v my-vol:/app my-image Create data inside the container: docker exec -it my-cont-1 bash cd /app echo "This is my delta data" > file.txt cat file.txt # Output: This is my delta data Verify Persistence: Delete the container and check the volume data directly on the host. docker rm -f my-cont-1 sudo cat /var/lib/docker/volumes/my-vol/_data/file.txt # Output: This is my delta data The data persists even though the container is gone.

Type Use Case Pros Cons Named Volume Default Docker-managed volumes (e.g., my-vol). Easy to use, portable, survives container deletion. Abstracted path, may need extra step for backups. Bind Mount Mount a specific host directory to the container. Full control, real-time syncing, easy for dev work. Tied to host path, can cause permission issues. tmpfs Mount Temporary in-memory mount (data lost on restart). Fast, doesn't write to disk. Data not persistent, only useful for short-term use. Preference: Named Volumes are preferred in most production use-cases because they are managed, portable, and persistent. Bind Mounts are useful for development/local testing to sync code from your machine into the container.
Ephemeral storage refers to storage that is temporary, meaning any data written to it only lasts for the duration of the Pod's lifetime. When the Pod is deleted or evicted, the data is lost.

Type Scope/Lifetime Key Feature Use Cases EmptyDir Pod Lifecycle Created on the node's local disk or RAM. Enables inter-container data sharing. Scratch space, caching, large temporary computations. Downward API Pod Lifecycle Exposes Pod metadata (IP, Name, Labels) to the container. Dynamic configuration, logging, self-awareness. ConfigMap & Secret Independent but mounted per Pod Injects configuration or sensitive data into the Pod filesystem. Decoupling config from code, managing credentials. Generic Ephemeral Volumes Pod Lifecycle Allows using PVC-like features (snapshotting, specific backends) for temporary storage. High-performance temporary storage requiring specific disk types (SSD).

An emptyDir volume is first created when a Pod is assigned to a Node, and exists as long as that Pod is running on that node. Inter-container Sharing: All containers in the Pod can read and write the same files in the emptyDir volume. Isolation: If a Deployment has 3 replicas, each Pod gets its own isolated emptyDir. They do not share data between Pods.

By default, emptyDir is stored on the node's disk (HDD/SSD). For high-performance workloads, you can force it into the node's RAM (tmpfs). Note: RAM-backed storage counts against the container's memory limit. If the node reboots, the data is wiped. Example YAML (Disk vs. RAM): apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: cache-pod spec: containers: - name: nginx image: nginx volumeMounts: - name: ram-storage mountPath: /cache volumes: - name: ram-storage emptyDir: medium: Memory # This forces the storage into RAM (tmpfs) sizeLimit: "1Gi" # Optional: Prevents the Pod from consuming too much RAM

The Downward API allows Pods to access their own metadata without making calls to the Kubernetes API server. Why use it? Security: Containers don't need a ServiceAccount with API permissions just to find out their own name or IP. Configuration: Useful for logging agents that need to tag logs with the Pod Name or Namespace.

Method A: Environment Variables (fieldRef)​ env: - name: MY_POD_IP valueFrom: fieldRef: fieldPath: status.podIP Method B: Volume Files (downwardAPI volume)​ This creates a file inside the container containing the metadata value. volumes: - name: pod-info downwardAPI: items: - path: "labels" fieldRef: fieldPath: metadata.labels

While often used as environment variables, mounting them as volumes is more robust: Dynamic Updates: If a ConfigMap is updated, the file inside the Pod is eventually updated by the Kubelet (usually within 60 seconds) without a Pod restart. (Env vars require a restart). Binary Data: Secrets can store binary files (like SSH keys or certificates) which are difficult to handle as env vars.

Introduced to provide "scratch space" that supports features usually reserved for Persistent Volumes (like specific StorageClasses or Snapshots). They are created when the Pod is created and deleted when the Pod is deleted. They allow you to request a specific amount of space (e.g., 20Gi) from a specific storage provider (e.g., EBS or local-path). spec: containers: - name: app image: busybox volumeMounts: - mountPath: /scratch name: ephemeral-scratch volumes: - name: ephemeral-scratch ephemeral: volumeClaimTemplate: spec: storageClassName: "gp3" # Use a specific fast SSD class accessModes: [ "ReadWriteOnce" ] resources: requests: storage: 2Gi

Just like CPU and Memory, you can (and should) manage how much disk space a Pod can consume on the node's local disk to prevent one Pod from filling up the entire node. spec: containers: - name: app resources: requests: ephemeral-storage: "1Gi" limits: ephemeral-storage: "2Gi" Request: Used by the scheduler to find a node with enough disk space. Limit: If the Pod exceeds this (via emptyDir or container logs), the Kubelet will evict the Pod.

Lifetime: Always tied to the Pod. If the Pod dies/is deleted, the data is gone. emptyDir: Use for data sharing between containers in one Pod. RAM disk: Use medium: Memory for sub-millisecond latency caching. Limits: Always set ephemeral-storage limits in production to prevent "No space left on device" errors on your nodes. Downward API: It is the "Self-Awareness" tool for Pods.
Persistent Storage refers to data that exists independently of any single Pod's lifecycle.

Kubernetes storage management has evolved from In-Tree plugins to the modern CSI standard. 1. In-Tree Volume Plugins (Legacy Model - Deprecated)​ Historically: Storage Drivers were embedded directly in the Kubernetes core. Drawbacks: Maintenance was cumbersome and tied to Kubernetes release cycles. Vendors could not independently develop or release updates. Bugs in storage drivers could affect the Kubernetes core functionality. Examples (Legacy): AWS EBS, Google Persistent Disk, Azure Disk and File Storage, Cinder, Ceph. Example PV (In-Tree): Note the driver specification within the spec. apiVersion: v1 kind: PersistentVolume metadata: name: in-tree-pv spec: capacity: storage: 10Gi accessModes: ReadWriteOnce awsElasticBlockStore: # Legacy in-tree driver section volumeID: vol-0abcd1234efgh5678 fsType: ext4 Note: Most in-tree plugins were officially deprecated starting with Kubernetes 1.21. 2. CSI Backed (Container Storage Interface) - The Modern Standard​ CSI: Developed by the CNCF, it decouples storage driver development from the Kubernetes core. Key Benefits of CSI: Independent Updates: Vendors can release drivers without waiting for Kubernetes core updates. Faster Development: Features and fixes are delivered more quickly. Flexibility: Supports advanced capabilities like snapshotting, resizing, cloning, and monitoring. Easy Integration: Simpler for vendors to develop custom drivers. Confirmation: Check the provisioner field in the StorageClass or look at csidrivers to confirm a CSI driver is in use. Example PV (CSI Backed): Note the modern csi section. apiVersion: v1 kind: PersistentVolume metadata: name: csi-pv spec: capacity: storage: 10Gi accessModes: ReadWriteOnce storageClassName: gp3-sc # Links to a StorageClass that uses a CSI driver csi: # Modern CSI driver section driver: ebs.csi.aws.com volumeHandle: vol-0abcd1234efgh5678 fsType: ext4 Object Storage Note: Kubernetes does not natively support mounting Object Storage (like Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage) as volumes because it operates differently from file systems. Applications should use vendor-specific SDKs or APIs to interact with object storage.

CSI drivers enable access to different types of storage: 1. File Storage​ Structure: Stored in a hierarchical structure (folders/directories). Also known as shared storage. Access: Requires file name + full file path to retrieve a file. Examples: Used in NAS (Network Attached Storage). Protocols include NFS and SMB. Characteristics: Simple, easy, and inexpensive. 2. Block Storage​ Usage: Used for large and structured files like databases and applications. Structure: The file is divided into multiple blocks, each with a unique ID. Blocks can be spread across different disk drives. Examples: Commonly used with SAN (Storage Area Network). Protocols include iSCSI and FC (Fibre Channel). Characteristics: Faster and more flexible than file storage, but more complex. 3. Object Storage​ Usage: Used for large amounts of unstructured data. Components: Every object has 3 parts: ID (unique identifier), metadata (description), and data (actual data). Access: Easily available via HTTP Requests. Use Cases: Storing static content like photos, music, backups, etc.

Mechanism: A hostPath volume mounts files or directories directly from the host node's filesystem into the Pod. Node-Specific: hostPath volumes are limited to the node where the Pod is scheduled. All Pods on the same node can access the data, but Pods on different nodes cannot share the same hostPath. Use Cases: Debugging, accessing host-level files (logs, configuration), or sharing specific host resources with containers.

Security Risks: Pods can potentially access sensitive host files if the path is misconfigured. Limited Portability: Being tied to a specific node reduces scheduling flexibility—the Pod can only run on the node that has the data. Better Alternatives: PersistentVolumes (PV) with PersistentVolumeClaims (PVC) or Local Persistent Volumes are recommended for persistent data as they offer better control and security abstraction.

When running Kubernetes in environments like KIND (which uses a Docker container as a node, running on macOS/Windows): Platform Docker Engine Runs On hostPath Points To Ubuntu/Linux Natively Host's actual filesystem (e.g., /tmp/hostfile) macOS/Windows Linux VM via Docker Filesystem inside the Kubernetes node container (the Linux VM) Example hostPath Pod: apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: hostpath-example spec: containers: - name: busybox-container image: busybox command: ["sh", "-c", "cat /data && sleep 3600"] # Reads /data volumeMounts: - name: host-volume mountPath: /data # Container mounts host file here volumes: - name: host-volume hostPath: path: /tmp/hostfile type: FileOrCreate # If the file doesn't exist on the host, create it. Data Population: Data is written to the host file via the container: kubectl exec -it hostpath-example -- sh -c 'echo "Hey you!!" > /data' Verification: A second Pod scheduled on the same node can read the data: kubectl exec hostpath-verify -- cat /data # Expected Output: Hey you!!
documents.s: Understanding hostPath in KIND (Linux VM context)

documents.t: A PV is a piece of storage in your cluster that has been provisioned either manually by an administrator or dynamically using Storage Classes. PVs exist independently of Pod lifecycles and can be reused or retained even after the Pod is deleted. They have properties such as capacity, access modes, and reclaim policies.

A PVC is a request for storage by a user. It functions similarly to how a Pod requests compute resources. When a PVC is created, Kubernetes searches for a PV that meets the claim's requirements. Binding Process:​ Administrator: Provisions PVs (or sets up Storage Classes for dynamic provisioning). Developer: Creates a PVC in the Pod specification requesting specific storage attributes. Kubernetes: Binds the PVC to a suitable PV, thereby making the storage available to the Pod. Pods rely on Node resources—such as CPU, memory, and network—to run containers. On the other hand, when a Pod requires persistent storage, it uses a PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) to request storage from a PersistentVolume (PV), which serves as the actual storage backend.

1. PVs are Cluster-Scoped Resources​ A PersistentVolume (PV) is a cluster-wide resource, just like Nodes or StorageClasses. This means it is not tied to any specific namespace, and it can be viewed or managed from anywhere within the cluster. You can verify this using: kubectl api-resources | grep persistentvolume This shows that the resource persistentvolumes has no namespace, indicating it's cluster-scoped. 2. PVCs are Namespace-Scoped​ A PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC), on the other hand, is a namespaced resource, just like Pods or Deployments. This means it exists within a specific namespace and is only accessible by workloads (Pods) within that namespace. You can verify this using: kubectl api-resources | grep persistentvolumeclaim Example: If you have a namespace called app1-ns and a PVC is created there and binds to a PV, only Pods in app1-ns can use that PVC. If a Pod in app2-ns tries to reference the same PVC, it will fail because the PVC is invisible outside its namespace. 3. 1-to-1 Binding Relationship Between PVC and PV​ A PVC can bind to only one PV. Similarly, a PV can be bound to only one PVC. This is a strict one-to-one relationship, ensuring data integrity and predictable access control. Once a PV is bound, its claimRef field is populated, and it cannot be claimed by any other PVC unless explicitly released. claimRef: This is a field in a PersistentVolume (PV) that records which PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) has successfully claimed it. It includes details like the PVC’s name and namespace. This field ensures that the PV is not mistakenly claimed by any other PVC. 4. PVCs request storage​ PVs fulfill that request if they match capacity, access mode, and storage class. Once a PVC is bound, it remains bound until: The PVC is deleted. The PV is manually reclaimed or deleted (depending on the reclaim policy). The reclaim policy (Retain, Delete, or deprecated Recycle) determines what happens to the PV after the PVC is deleted.

Step Role Action Details / Notes 1 Developer Requests 5Gi persistent storage for a Pod. May request via a PVC or through communication with the Kubernetes Admin. 2 Kubernetes Admin Coordinates with Storage Admin for backend volume. Backend storage could be SAN/NAS exposed via iSCSI, NFS, etc. 3 Storage Admin Allocates a physical volume from a 500Ti storage pool. May involve LUN creation, NFS export, etc., based on the infrastructure. 4 Kubernetes Admin Creates a PersistentVolume (PV) representing the physical volume in Kubernetes. Specifies capacity, accessModes, volumeMode, storageClassName, etc. 5 Developer Creates a PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) requesting 5Gi with specific access and volume modes. PVC must match criteria defined in the PV. 6 Kubernetes Binds PVC to a suitable PV if all parameters match. Matching criteria include: storage class, access mode, volume mode, size, etc. 7 Pod References the PVC in its volume definition and mounts it in a container. PVC acts as an abstraction; Pod doesn't interact with the PV directly.

Access Mode Description Example Use Case Type of Storage & Examples ReadWriteOnce (RWO) The volume can be mounted as read-write by a single node. Multiple Pods can access it only if they are on the same node. Databases that require exclusive access but may run multiple replicas per node. Block Storage (e.g., Amazon EBS, GCP Persistent Disk, Azure Managed Disks) ReadOnlyMany (ROX) The volume can be mounted as read-only by multiple nodes simultaneously. Sharing static data like configuration files or read-only datasets across multiple nodes. File Storage (e.g., NFS, Azure File Storage) ReadWriteMany (RWX) The volume can be mounted as read-write by multiple nodes simultaneously. Content management systems, shared data applications, or log aggregation. File Storage (e.g., Amazon EFS, Azure File Storage, On-Prem NFS) ReadWriteOncePod (RWOP) (v1.29+) The volume can be mounted as read-write by only one Pod across the entire cluster. Ensuring exclusive access to a volume for a single Pod, such as in tightly controlled workloads. Block Storage (e.g., Amazon EBS with RWOP enforcement)

Block Storage​ Ideal for: Databases and applications requiring low-latency, high-performance storage. It provides raw storage blocks that applications can format and manage as individual disks. Examples: Amazon EBS, GCP Persistent Disk, Dell EMC Block Storage. Key Characteristic: Block storage is generally node-specific and does not support simultaneous multi-node access. Access Modes: Commonly used with ReadWriteOnce or ReadWriteOncePod. Analogy: Like attaching a USB drive to a single computer—it provides fast, reliable storage but cannot be shared concurrently across multiple systems. File Storage​ Ideal for: Shared storage scenarios where multiple Pods or applications need simultaneous access to the same data. It is mounted as a shared filesystem. Examples: Amazon EFS, Azure File Storage, On-Prem NFS (Network File System). Key Characteristic: Purpose-built for multi-node concurrent access. Access Modes: Often supports ReadOnlyMany or ReadWriteMany.

Reclaim Policy Behavior Best Use Case Common in Delete Deletes PV and storage resource when PVC is deleted. Cloud-based dynamically provisioned storage. AWS EBS, GCP PD, Azure Disk. Retain Keeps PV and storage, requiring manual cleanup. Backup, auditing, manual data recovery. On-prem storage, long-term retention workloads. Recycle (Deprecated) Cleans volume and makes PV available again. (Not recommended) Previously used in legacy systems.

Condition Requirement for Binding Storage Class Match storageClassName of PVC and PV must match (or both can be empty). Access Mode Compatibility PVC's requested access mode must be supported by PV. Sufficient Capacity PV's storage must be ≥ PVC's requested capacity. Volume Binding Mode Either Immediate or WaitForFirstConsumer. Volume State PV must be in Available state to bind. Matching Volume Mode PVC and PV must have the same volumeMode (Filesystem or Block). Claim Reference If PV has a claimRef, it can only bind to that specific PVC.

1. Delete existing storage classes: kubectl delete sc --all 2. Create a PV (example-pv.yaml): apiVersion: v1 kind: PersistentVolume metadata: name: example-pv # Unique name for the PV spec: capacity: storage: 5Gi # Total storage provided accessModes: - ReadWriteOnce # Mounted as read-write by a single node persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain # Retain the volume and data after PVC deletion hostPath: path: /mnt/data # Uses a directory on the node (for demo purposes only) Note: When ReclaimPolicy is set to Retain, the PV and its data will not be deleted if the PVC is removed. The storage is preserved for manual recovery and must be handled by an admin before reuse. 3. Create a PVC (example-pvc.yaml): apiVersion: v1 kind: PersistentVolumeClaim metadata: name: example-pvc # Unique name for the PVC spec: accessModes: - ReadWriteOnce # Request volume to be mounted as read-write by a single node resources: requests: storage: 2Gi # Ask for at least 2Gi of storage Note: Since this PVC doesn't specify a StorageClass, it binds to a compatible PV. The 5Gi PV created above is a suitable candidate for this 2Gi claim. 4. Create the Pod referencing the PVC (example-pod.yaml): apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: example-pod spec: containers: - name: nginx-container image: nginx volumeMounts: - mountPath: /usr/share/nginx/html # Directory inside container where volume is mounted name: persistent-storage # Logical name for the volume mount volumes: - name: persistent-storage # Volume name referenced above persistentVolumeClaim: claimName: example-pvc # Bind this volume to the previously created PVC When this Pod is created, Kubernetes binds the PVC to the PV and mounts the volume. The PVC status changes from "Pending" to "Bound". Important Note on Deletion: To delete a PV or PVC, you must delete the Pod first, then the PVC, and finally the PV. Otherwise, resources may remain in a "Terminating" state due to Kubernetes safety mechanisms. Verification Commands: kubectl get pv kubectl describe pv example-pv kubectl get pvc kubectl describe pvc example-pvc kubectl describe pod example-pod

A Storage Class in Kubernetes defines different storage configurations, enabling dynamic provisioning of PVs. It eliminates the need to manually pre-create PVs. Purpose: Define storage backends (disk types), reclaim policies, and binding modes. Dynamic Provisioning: When a PVC is created, Kubernetes uses the referenced Storage Class to automatically provision a corresponding PV. Flexibility: Multiple Storage Classes (e.g., high-performance SSDs, low-cost HDD) can coexist. Note: StorageClass replaces manual PV provisioning. However, attributes like accessModes, size, and volumeMode are still defined in the PVC. AWS EBS Storage Class Examples:​ General Purpose (gp3): apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1 kind: StorageClass metadata: name: ebs-sc-gp3 provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com parameters: type: gp3 reclaimPolicy: Delete volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer High Performance (io1): apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1 kind: StorageClass metadata: name: ebs-sc-io1 provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com parameters: type: io1 reclaimPolicy: Delete volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer

PVC Creation: apiVersion: v1 kind: PersistentVolumeClaim metadata: name: example-pvc spec: accessModes: - ReadWriteOnce resources: requests: storage: 2Gi Even if no storageClassName is specified, Kubernetes defaults to the "standard" StorageClass (if configured as default). The PVC status remains "Pending" until a Pod is created. Verify Default StorageClass: kubectl describe sc standard Look for the annotation: storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true". The WaitForFirstConsumer Binding Mode:​ This mode is critical because it delays PV creation until a Pod is scheduled. Cost Optimization: Ensures resources aren't provisioned until actually needed. Zonal Awareness: In multi-AZ environments (like AWS), it ensures the volume is created in the same Availability Zone where the Pod is scheduled. Without this, a PVC might trigger volume creation in AZ-1 while the Pod is scheduled in AZ-2, making the volume inaccessible. Pod referencing the PVC: apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: example-pod spec: containers: - name: nginx-container image: nginx volumeMounts: - mountPath: /usr/share/nginx/html name: persistent-storage volumes: - name: persistent-storage persistentVolumeClaim: claimName: example-pvc Once the Pod is created, Kubernetes finds the PVC, provisions a PV using the default StorageClass, and the PVC status changes to Bound. Final Verification:​ # Check PVs kubectl get pv # Example output: pvc-24d1f4ee... 2Gi RWO Delete Bound default/example-pvc # Check PVCs kubectl get pvc # Example output: example-pvc Bound pvc-24d1f4ee... 2Gi RWO standard

A single codebase containing UI, business logic, and database where all the components will be tightly coupled. Simple to start, but hard to scale, update, and maintain. Challenges: Tightly coupled components. Downtime during upgrades. Inefficient scaling. Slower development due to cross-dependencies.

This is a common architectural pattern that logically separates the application into presentation, business logic, and data layers. Tier Description Technologies Frontend (Web Tier) User interface HTML, CSS, JS, React, Angular, Vue.js Middleware tier Manages APIs, logging, authentication, service coordination Express.js, Nginx, Kafka, RabbitMQ Backend (App Tier) Business logic, data processing Java, Python, Node.js, Go, .NET Database (Data Tier) Storing, processing and retrieving unstructured and structured data. MySQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Redis

Single-Server Model All tiers run on one machine. Pros and cons: Simple but not scalable or fault-tolerant. Three-Server Model Each tier on separate physical servers. Pros and cons: Better performance and fault isolation, but costly. Virtualized Deployment Tiers run in VMs on a single machine. Pros and cons: More affordable, scalable, and isolated. Cloud and Kubernetes Apps run in containers orchestrated by Kubernetes. Frontend, backend, and services are deployed independently (stateless services). Pros and cons: Databases often remain outside Kubernetes in managed services (e.g., AWS RDS). Challenges with 3-Tier Architecture (that Microservices/K8s aim to solve)​ Inefficient tier-level scaling (scaling must be done for the whole tier). Single point of failure (SPOF), which can cause the entire system to stop working if a tier fails. Tight coupling within tiers. Slower deployment cycles. Tech stack limitations within a tier (hard to introduce new languages/frameworks). Note: This 3-tier architecture can be run as a monolith (MVC framework) or deployed as microservices. It is just a design pattern.

Breaks down a monolithic app into independent services where each service can be scaled and updated independently. Example Services in E-Commerce:​ User Service Product Service Order Service Wishlist Service Advantages:​ Independent scaling (only scale the service under load). Fault isolation (failure in one service doesn't necessarily bring down others). Faster deployments (smaller codebases deploy quicker). Polyglot architecture (different services can use the best-suited technology stack). Easier maintenance.
Each service runs in its own Deployment workload object. They can be auto-scaled via HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler).

Databases are often hosted outside Kubernetes due to: Stateful complexity (managing persistent state is harder than stateless). Performance needs. Easier HA and backup via managed services (AWS RDS, GCP SQL). When to run DB in K8s:​ Testing or development environments. Using operators (e.g., MySQL/PostgreSQL Operator) to manage complexity. Small-scale self-managed setups. StatefulSets are the primary Kubernetes object used to manage stateful workloads like databases inside Kubernetes, ensuring unique network identities and ordered deployment/scaling/deletion.
Definition: Directly issue commands to modify cluster state. Focuses on how to achieve changes. Use Cases: Quick debugging, one-off tasks, learning.

Definition: Define the desired state in YAML/JSON manifests. Kubernetes reconciles the actual state to match the desired state. Use Cases: Production environments, CI/CD, version-controlled infrastructure.

These commands are useful for quickly interacting with the cluster or generating manifests. --dry-run: By default, as soon as the command is run, the resource will be created. If you simply want to test your command, use the --dry-run=client option. This will not create the resource; instead, it tells you whether the resource can be created and if your command syntax is correct. -o yaml: This will output the resource definition in YAML format on screen. You can use these two options in combination to generate a resource definition file quickly, which you can then modify and create resources from, instead of creating the files from scratch.

Create an NGINX Pod (Imperative): kubectl run nginx --image=nginx Generate POD Manifest YAML file (-o yaml). Don't create it (--dry-run=client): kubectl run nginx --image=nginx --dry-run=client -o yaml

Create a deployment (Imperative): kubectl create deployment --image=nginx nginx Generate Deployment YAML file (-o yaml). Don't create it (--dry-run=client): kubectl create deployment --image=nginx nginx --dry-run=client -o yaml Generate Deployment with 4 Replicas: kubectl create deployment nginx --image=nginx --replicas=4 Scale a deployment using the kubectl scale command: kubectl scale deployment nginx --replicas=4 Save the YAML definition to a file and modify it later: kubectl create deployment nginx --image=nginx --dry-run=client -o yaml > nginx-deployment.yaml You can then update the YAML file with the replicas or any other field before creating the deployment.

Create a Service named redis-service of type ClusterIP to expose pod redis on port 6379: kubectl expose pod redis --port=6379 --name=redis-service --dry-run=client -o yaml (This will automatically use the pod's labels as selectors). OR kubectl create service clusterip redis --tcp=6379:6379 --dry-run=client -o yaml (This will not use the pod's labels as selectors, instead it assumes selectors like app=redis. This can cause issues if your pod has a different label set. It's recommended to generate the file and modify selectors manually before creation.) Create a Service named nginx of type NodePort to expose pod nginx's port 80 on port 30080 on the nodes: kubectl expose pod nginx --type=NodePort --port=80 --name=nginx-service --dry-run=client -o yaml (This automatically uses the pod's labels as selectors, but you cannot specify the NodePort via expose. You must generate the file and manually add the nodePort field before creation.) OR kubectl create service nodeport nginx --tcp=80:80 --node-port=30080 --dry-run=client -o yaml (This will not use the pod's labels as selectors.) Recommendation: Both imperative commands have challenges. For specifying a NodePort, generate the definition file using kubectl expose and manually input the nodePort before creating the service.

When using kubectl apply, Kubernetes internally manages three states to determine what changes to make to the live resource: Name Location Purpose Local Object Definition Your YAML file (.yaml) What you want the resource to be (your desired state). Last Applied Configuration Stored in annotations on the object Snapshot of the last time you ran kubectl apply. Live Object Configuration Stored in the cluster The current actual state of the resource in the cluster.
documents.s: HOW KUBECTL APPLY WORKS IN THE BACKEND

documents.t: apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: httpd labels: type: web-server spec: app: my-app containers: - name: nginx-web-server image: nginx:1.17 When you run kubectl apply -f local-object-definition.yml and the object does not exist, it is created. When created, a "live object configuration" (the initial actual state) is also generated with status fields added.

When you use kubectl apply, it performs a three-way merge comparison: Local Object Definition, Last Applied Configuration, and Live Object Configuration. Updates: If the image is updated locally (e.g., to nginx:1.18), the difference between the Local and Live configurations is computed, and the live configuration is updated. Crucial for Deletions: The Last Applied Configuration is essential for detecting fields that were deleted from your local YAML file. If a field (like a label) exists in the Last Applied Configuration but is missing from the Local Object Definition, kubectl apply knows that field must be removed from the Live Object Configuration. If a field is in Live but missing from both Local and Last Applied, it is left alone.

A POD creates a logical layer to group one or more containers to have a common network namespace and shared storage. It is the single instance of an application and the smallest object you can create in Kubernetes. Pods have a one-to-one relationship with containers running the application. To scale up, you create new pods; to scale down, you delete existing pods. You do not add additional containers to an existing pod (except in the case of multi-container pods/helper containers). A Pod has a unique IP address assigned from the cluster's Pod network CIDR (e.g., --pod-network-cidr=10.244.0.0/16). This IP address is ephemeral; if the Pod gets deleted, the IP is removed. Containers inside a Pod talk to each other on localhost/127.0.0.1:<port_no> because they share the same network stack. The port number for each container must be unique to aid in communication. Replication of data among containers inside the Pod can be achieved using shared storage. You need to create containers inside a POD which are dependent to each other in some way.

To create a pod with an nginx image from the DockerHub repository: kubectl run nginx --image nginx To get the pods: kubectl get pods To get pods with their IP or with yaml/json output: kubectl get po -o wide kubectl get po -o yaml To delete and recreate an existing pod: kubectl replace --force -f app.yaml To get all the pods in a particular namespace: kubectl get po -n <namespace> To get detailed information about a pod (labels, containers, events): kubectl describe pod <pod-name> To check logs of a pod: kubectl logs po <podname> kubectl logs po <podname> -c <containername> To delete a pod (Pods are ephemeral): kubectl delete po <podname> To apply a yaml file: kubectl create -f app.yaml # Creates the resource kubectl apply -f app.yaml # Creates or updates the resource

Parameters:​ Field Description apiVersion Defines the Kubernetes API version (for Pod, it is usually v1). kind Type of object being created. For a pod, it is Pod. metadata Contains identifying data like name, labels, etc. metadata.name Name of the pod (must be DNS-compliant). spec Main configuration block for the pod. spec.containers List of containers in the pod. Each pod must have at least one container. containers.name Name of the container inside the pod. containers.image Docker image to run in the container (e.g., nginx, busybox). Example Pod YAML:​ apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: my-app-pod labels: app: my-app environment: dev spec: containers: - name: main-container image: nginx:1.23.4 ports: - containerPort: 80 name: http protocol: TCP env: - name: ENV_VAR_1 value: "value1" - name: ENV_VAR_2 value: "value2" resources: requests: memory: "64Mi" cpu: "250m" limits: memory: "128Mi" cpu: "500m" volumeMounts: - name: config-volume mountPath: /etc/config - name: data-volume mountPath: /var/data volumes: - name: config-volume configMap: name: app-config - name: data-volume emptyDir: {}

What is a ReplicationController?​ Ensures that a specified number of pod replicas are always running. If a pod crashes or is deleted, the RC will create a new one. It is an older concept, replaced by ReplicaSet, but still available. Key Features:​ Used to maintain pod availability. Watches pod health and replaces failed pods automatically. Cannot manage pods created manually (outside its definition). Pods are matched using selector labels. Example ReplicationController YAML:​ apiVersion: v1 kind: ReplicationController metadata: name: myapp-rc spec: replicas: 3 selector: app: myapp template: metadata: labels: app: myapp spec: containers: - name: myapp-container image: nginx ports: - containerPort: 80 Commands:​ Create RC: kubectl apply -f rc.yaml List RCs: kubectl get rc Describe RC: kubectl describe rc myapp-rc View managed pods: kubectl get pods -l app=myapp Delete RC (pods also go): kubectl delete rc myapp-rc

What is a ReplicaSet?​ Next-generation ReplicationController. Maintains a stable set of replica pods. Supports set-based selectors (more powerful). Backbone of Deployments in modern Kubernetes. Key Features:​ Maintains desired pod count. Matches pods using label selectors. Commonly used indirectly via Deployments. Example ReplicaSet YAML:​ apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: ReplicaSet metadata: name: myapp-rs spec: replicas: 2 selector: matchExpressions: - key: tier operator: In values: - frontend - backend template: metadata: labels: app: myapp tier: frontend spec: containers: - name: nginx-container image: nginx ports: - containerPort: 80 Commands:​ To get all replicasets: kubectl get rs -o wide To get all pods with labels: kubectl get po -o wide --show-labels To scale out: kubectl scale --replicas=5 rs/nginx-demo-rs To edit the replicaset: kubectl edit rs/nginx-demo-rs To delete the replicaset with pods: kubectl delete rs nginx-demo-rs To delete the replicaset without the pods (Orphan): kubectl delete --cascade=orphan rs nginx-demo-rs To unlabel a pod: kubectl label po <podname> app- (Unlabel a pod) To label/re-label a pod again: kubectl label po <podname> app=nginx [--overwrite] (Label/re-label a pod)

What is a Deployment?​ A higher-level abstraction that manages ReplicaSets, which in turn manage Pods. Flow: Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pods. Supports 2 update strategies: Rolling updates (zero downtime, gradually replaces old pods with new ones). Recreate (Stops all old pods, then starts new ones, causes downtime). Strategy Parameters (for RollingUpdate): maxUnavailable: (Default 25%) Max number/percentage of Pods that can be unavailable during the update. maxSurge: (Default 25%) Max number/percentage of Pods that can be created above the desired number of Pods during an update. Supports Rollout (upgrading to a higher version) and Rollback (reverting to an older version). Deployments add a pod-template-hash label to the ReplicaSets they create (and thus to the pods). This hash distinguishes between different revisions (default revisionHistoryLimit: 10). Do not modify this label. Example Deployment YAML:​ apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: myapp-deployment spec: replicas: 3 selector: matchLabels: app: myapp strategy: type: RollingUpdate rollingUpdate: maxSurge: 1 maxUnavailable: 1 template: metadata: labels: app: myapp spec: containers: - name: myapp-container image: nginx:1.21 ports: - containerPort: 80 COMMANDS:​ Action Command View details of a deployment kubectl describe deployment <name> View YAML of deployment kubectl get deployment <name> -o yaml Edit deployment live kubectl edit deployment <name> Delete deployment kubectl delete deployment <name> Scale deployment kubectl scale deployment <name> --replicas=4 Update image (rolling update) kubectl set image deployment/<name> <container>=<new-image> Pause rollout kubectl rollout pause deployment <name> Resume rollout kubectl rollout resume deployment <name> Check rollout status kubectl rollout status deployment <name> View rollout history kubectl rollout history deployment <name> Rollback to previous version kubectl rollout undo deployment <name> Rollback to specific revision kubectl rollout undo deployment <name> --to-revision=<rev>

Kubernetes Pods are ephemeral; they can be created, destroyed, or rescheduled at any time. Each pod gets its own IP address, but these IPs are not stable. Services provide a stable network endpoint and load balancing mechanism to access a group of pods, abstracting away the dynamic nature of pod lifecycles.

A Service identifies its backend Pods by using labels, defined under a selector (e.g., app=A). Every Service has an IP address called a Virtual IP Address (VIP) and a DNS Name. We can create different Services using the .spec.type field: ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer, etc. Backend Pods are integrated with the Service using the EndPoint object (or EndpointSlice object). Service DNS names are controlled by the CoreDNS add-on in the k8s cluster. Default protocols supported by a Service are: TCP, UDP, SCTP. A Service can be identified by two primary modes: Environment variables (inside the container of the pod) and DNS (<service-name>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local).

Type Access Scope Description ClusterIP Internal (default) Accessible only within the cluster. NodePort External via <NodeIP>:<port> Exposes the service on a static port on each node. LoadBalancer External via cloud LB (AWS/GCP) Creates an external cloud provider load balancer. ExternalName Maps to an external DNS name Does DNS aliasing, no selector, does not proxy traffic.

Purpose: Exposes the service on an internal IP address within the cluster. Used for communication between services inside the cluster. Why Use It: Default service type; provides secure, private communication without exposing to external traffic. How to Access: Via the spec.clusterIP IP address (e.g., http://<cluster-ip>:<port>). Example: A backend database service (e.g., MySQL) accessed only by application pods within the cluster. ClusterIP Example YAML:​ apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: database-service spec: type: ClusterIP selector: app: mysql ports: - port: 3306 targetPort: 3306 This service makes a MySQL database accessible only to other services within the cluster at database-service:3306. To test it, you need an utility pod and use nslookup <clusterip>.

Purpose: Exposes the service on the same port across all worker nodes. It extends ClusterIP by allowing external traffic. Why Use It: When external access is needed but without a cloud provider's load balancer (e.g., in dev/test environments). Note: NodePort IP can only be between 30000 to 32767. How to Access: Via any node's IP address and the assigned nodePort (e.g., http://<node-ip>:30007). Example: Testing a web application (e.g., NGINX) externally in a non-cloud environment. NodePort Example YAML:​ apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: web-app-nodeport spec: type: NodePort selector: app: web-app ports: - port: 80 targetPort: 8080 nodePort: 30080 This exposes a web application on port 30080 of every cluster node, accessible via http://<node-ip>:30080.

Purpose: Integrates with cloud providers (e.g., AWS, GCP) to create an external load balancer. Why Use It: For production-grade external access with high availability, SSL termination, and advanced routing. How to Access: Via the cloud provider's load balancer IP (e.g., http://<loadbalancer-ip>:<port>). Example: Public-facing web application (e.g., an e-commerce site) requiring global accessibility. LoadBalancer Example YAML:​ apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: web-app-loadbalancer spec: type: LoadBalancer selector: app: web-app ports: - port: 80 targetPort: 8080 This creates a cloud load balancer that distributes traffic to web application pods, providing a stable external IP address.

Purpose: Maps the service to an external DNS name, acting as a CNAME record. Why Use It: Allows services within the cluster to access external services using Kubernetes service discovery mechanisms. It doesn't proxy traffic but provides DNS resolution. When to Use: Accessing external databases or APIs. Migrating services gradually (some internal, some external). Creating service abstractions for external dependencies. ExternalName Example YAML:​ apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: external-database spec: type: ExternalName externalName: db.example.com
A namespace is a virtual cluster within a physical Kubernetes cluster, providing logical isolation for resources (Pods, Services, Deployments, etc.).

Resource Isolation: Separate environments (e.g., dev/prod). Avoid Name Collisions: The same resource name can exist in different namespaces. Access Control: Apply RBAC rules per namespace. Resource Quotas: Limit CPU/memory/storage per namespace. Not for Network Isolation: Use Network Policies instead for traffic control between namespaces. Note: Default Namespaces: default, kube-system, kube-public. Service DNS Format: <service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local.
apiVersion: v1 kind: Namespace metadata: name: my-app

Command Description kubectl create ns <name> Create a namespace kubectl get namespaces List all namespaces kubectl describe ns <name> Show namespace details kubectl delete ns <name> Delete a namespace (cascades to all resources within) kubectl get pods -n <ns> List pods in a specific namespace kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=<ns> Set default namespace for the current context Note on Checking Pod Namespace: To check which namespace a particular pod exists across the cluster: kubectl get po --all-namespaces # OR kubectl get po -A

Frontend YAML (frontend-deploy.yaml) applied to app1-ns: kubectl apply -f frontend-deploy.yaml -n app1-ns Backend YAML (backend-deploy.yaml) applied to app1-ns: kubectl apply -f backend-deploy.yaml -n app1-ns

documents.t: Test Pod in default Namespace (e.g., for testing outside namespaces): kubectl run test-pod --image=busybox -it --rm --restart=Never -- /bin/sh curl backend-svc:9090 # X Will not work (due to default namespace context) For cross-namespace access, use the fully qualified DNS format: curl http://backend-svc.app1-ns:9090 Format for Cross-Namespace Access: curl http://<service-name>.<namespace-name>:<service-port> <service-name>: Name of the Kubernetes Service (e.g., backend-svc). <namespace-name>: Namespace where the service is deployed (e.g., app1-ns). <service-port>: The ClusterIP port exposed by the service (e.g., 9090).

Why? It's cumbersome to use -n <namespace> with every command. You can set a default namespace in the current context. kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=app1-ns Now, you don't need to use -n app1-ns with every command. To check the current context: kubectl config get-contexts
documents.s: Setting a Default Namespace in Kubernetes Context

documents.t: Segregate Workloads: Separate dev, test, and prod environments. Use Namespaces for Multi-Tenancy: Avoid resource conflicts by isolating teams or projects. Resource Quotas: Set limits on CPU, memory, and storage per namespace. Namespace Naming Conventions: Use clear and consistent names (e.g., team-app-env $\rightarrow$ frontend-prod-ns). Avoid Manual Deletion: Use kubectl delete namespace carefully, as it removes all resources within it. Apply Network Policies: Secure namespaces by using network policies to control traffic flow.
